", N not looked at" : ""}`.
suggested_fix: Count by VERDICT, not by presence of a finding: only increment Assessed when `worstRank(a.worst) > worstRank(StatusUnknown)`; route a control whose worst verdict is Unknown into Unassessed (or a third `NoVerdict` counter surfaced as its own line) so Assessed+Unassessed+NoVerdict == ControlsWithCheck. Keep NotApplicable in its own bucket. The Note tail then stops contradicting the counters for free.

rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e; storagemeter is untouched by the 27 commits. When `_cat/indices` lists rows but every one fails `parseInt64(r.Store)` — a fully closed or relocating index set — the loop increments `sizeless` for each and adds nothing to byScope, so the empty-bucket branch fires and returns a MEASURED zero whose detail asserts 'the pattern this caller may enumerate matched no index'. That sentence is false: the pattern matched several indices whose bytes could not be read, and the `sizeless` counter that knows so is dropped on this path while the mixed path at :151-153 appends it correctly. The package's own doctrine names this as a defect, not a nicety: 'a total that is silently low is the same failure as a derived number labelled measured' (:104-107). rc1_blocking (narrow): customer-visible correctness / silent failure on a capacity surface — a tenant whose indices are all closed reads as holding zero bytes, with an explanation that rules out the real cause, which is the wrong input to a retention or ceiling decision. Severity stays low: it needs EVERY matched index to be sizeless, the surface is read-only, and it does not gate billing or enforcement.
evidence: probe.go:110-113 `bytes, ok := parseInt64(r.Store); if !ok { sizeless++; continue }`; probe.go:130-135 `if len(byScope) == 0 { return []Reading{measured(StoreOpenSearch, scopeOf(p), 0, ..., "measured: the pattern this caller may enumerate matched no index, so zero bytes is the MEASUREMENT, not a missing value", at, nil)} }` — `sizeless` is not consulted; contrast the correct mixed path, probe.go:151-153 `if sizeless > 0 { detail += ". " + itoa(sizeless) + " index(es) in this caller's pattern reported NO size (closed or relocating) and are excluded from the total rather than counted as zero" }`; stated invariant at probe.go:104-107.
suggested_fix: Guard the empty branch on `sizeless`: when `len(byScope) == 0 && sizeless > 0`, return `notMeasured(...)` (or a measured zero carrying the same sizeless caveat sentence the mixed path appends) naming the count of indices that reported no size. Two lines, no behaviour change for the genuine no-index case.

rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e. HandleStatus carefully scopes the row list — `"tenants": l.StatusFor(p.Tenant, p.Cross)` — and then, in the same body, serves `l.metrics.Snapshot()`, which is unconditionally platform-wide: it SUMS `m.runs` across every tenant segment and returns the global `truncated`, `emitFailures`, `deadLettered`, `lost`, `ungroundable` and per-evidence-class `emitted_*` counters. Any holder of the per-tenant admin gate (administration:write on its own tenant) reads them. This is an aggregate inference channel, not a row leak — but it contradicts the handler's own stated invariant three lines above it ('the mere existence of another tenant is not its to know'): a tenant admin that polls the endpoint around its own scans can difference the counters and derive that other tenants exist, how often they scan, and roughly how much evidence they emit per class. The existing isolation test does NOT cover this and is a textbook instance of the repo's test-double blind spot: `secLaneServer` runs `lane.ScanAll` over acme AND globex, so acme's response carries `scan_runs_total: 2`, yet the assertion is only `strings.Contains(w.Body.String(), "globex")` plus a row count — and the metrics map keys carry no tenant name, so it passes green. I ran `go test -run TestSecurityLaneStatusIsOwnTenantOnly ./` in src/backend: ok, 0.223s, with the aggregate block present. rc1_blocking: tenant isolation, per the rule that a LOW touching isolation still blocks.
evidence: http.go:24-26 (the invariant) `a tenant admin sees ONLY its own row, because the mere existence of another tenant is not its to know`; http.go:41-42 `"metrics": l.metrics.Snapshot(),` next to `"tenants": l.StatusFor(p.Tenant, p.Cross),`; metrics.go:127-139 `var runs int64; for _, v := range m.runs { runs += v }; out["scan_runs_total"] = runs; ... for _, c := range evidenceClasses { out["emitted_"+c] = m.emitted[c] }` — no scope parameter exists on Snapshot; the blind test: security_lane_isolation_test.go:66 `lane.ScanAll(context.Background())` (both tenants) then :85-87 `if strings.Contains(w.Body.String(), "globex") { t.Fatalf("TENANT LEAK: ...") }` and :91-94 which decode only `Tenants`, never `metrics`.
suggested_fix: Give Snapshot a scoped sibling — `SnapshotFor(seg string)` built from the per-segment `m.runs[seg\x00outcome]` keys `RunsFor` already indexes, with the per-class/dead-letter counters either tracked per segment or omitted for a non-cross caller — and serve the unscoped map only when `p.Cross`. Then extend security_lane_isolation_test.go to assert on the decoded `metrics` map (e.g. acme's `scan_runs_total` == 1 after a two-tenant ScanAll), since the current substring assertion cannot see this class of leak.

rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e (file untouched by the 27 post-review commits: `git log d796bf7d..9d981e5e -- src/backend/secapi/store.go` is empty). For a cross-tenant (Global) principal, `visible(tenant, cross, owner)` returns true for EVERY owner, and both backends then assign `out[id] = <that owner's value>` with no combination rule: the file backend ranges a Go map (iteration order randomized per range) and the pg backend reads `SELECT rule_id, enabled FROM security_rule_state` with no ORDER BY and no aggregate. Two tenants that disagree on one rule therefore produce a value that can differ between two identical GET /api/security/rules calls, and the handler renders it through `Apply(Catalog(), states)` as the platform's answer. The sibling surface in the same package solved exactly this and documented it, so the intended semantics are on record and the rule store simply does not implement them; the package also already treats non-determinism as a defect elsewhere (`byName` exists 'so a picker does not reshuffle between polls', store.go:121-122). Blast radius is bounded to the read: putRules refuses a cross-tenant write (http.go:958-966) and the scanning path always calls with cross=false (main.go:5473-5479, 'cross=false ALWAYS'), so detection behaviour is unaffected — this is a display/API-truth defect only. rc1_blocking because an API on the security surface returns a different answer to the same request and can tell a platform admin a detection rule is off when a tenant has it on (misleading security results / customer-visible correctness); the fix is a one-line union matching frameworks_store.go, so remediation risk is near zero.
evidence: store.go:284-291 `for owner, byRule := range s.rules { if !visible(tenant, cross, owner) { continue }; for id, r := range byRule { out[id] = r.Enabled } }` — plain assignment, unordered map. store.go:414 `tx.Query(ctx, "SELECT rule_id, enabled FROM security_rule_state")` then :427 `out[id] = enabled` — no ORDER BY, no aggregate. Contrast frameworks_store.go:176-180: `// A cross-tenant (platform) view sees the union: a framework any / visible tenant enabled reads as enabled. Nothing is hidden and / nothing is invented; the handler says whose view this is.` followed by `out[id] = out[id] || r.Enabled`. visible() is store.go:117-119 `return cross || owner == NormTenant(tenant)`.
suggested_fix: Fold with the framework store's documented rule — `out[id] = out[id] || r.Enabled` in FileStore.RuleStates, and `bool_or(enabled) ... GROUP BY rule_id` in the pg query — and carry the same comment so the two cross-tenant folds cannot drift.

where: src/backend/secapi/store.go:533 (pgStore.DeleteView) vs store.go:377-396 (FileStore.DeleteView), handler at src/backend/secapi/http.go:1126-1148
rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e (file unchanged since the review). The handler's only id check is `isSafeToken`, which accepts any 1..MaxTokenLen string of [A-Za-z0-9-_.:/()+] (filters.go:150-163) — 'abc' passes. The pg backend then hands that straight to `$1::uuid`, so Postgres raises 22P02 invalid_text_representation, DeleteView returns the error, and the handler answers 502 with the driver's message, which writeError echoes verbatim (main.go:4549-4551 `writeJSON(w, status, map[string]string{"error": err.Error()})`). The file backend returns (false, nil) for the same input and the handler answers 404. So the same request gets 404 on one store backend and 502-plus-SQLSTATE-text on the other — and PG is now the default store for fresh installs. NOT rc1-blocking: the query is parameterized (no injection), the cast fails before any row is touched so nothing is deleted and RLS/tenant scoping is unaffected, the failure is loud rather than silent, and the leaked text is a type-cast complaint, not data, credentials or another tenant's id. What is left is a wrong status code and internal-error text on a malformed input — API polish, cheap to fix, but none of the rc1 classes.
evidence: store.go:533 `tag, err := tx.Exec(ctx, `DELETE FROM security_saved_views WHERE id = $1::uuid`, id)`. http.go:1139-1141 `if !isSafeToken(id) { a.d.WriteError(w, http.StatusBadRequest, errors.New("invalid view id")); return }` — the only validation. http.go:1145-1147 `if err != nil { a.d.WriteError(w, http.StatusBadGateway, err); return }`. main.go:4549-4551 writeError echoes err.Error(). FileStore.DeleteView store.go:395 `return false, nil` → http.go:1149-1153 404.
suggested_fix: Validate the id as a UUID at the boundary (the ids are minted by newUUIDv4, store.go:95-103) and answer 404 for a well-formed-but-unknown id, 400 for a non-UUID — or map SQLSTATE 22P02 to found=false in pgStore.DeleteView so both backends answer identically.

rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e (neither SecurityOverview.tsx nor model.ts was touched by the 27 commits). `facetTotal` sums the VALUES of a facet map (model.ts:229-230), so `facetTotal(facets?.seam)` is the number of findings that carry a seam, not the number of seams. The committed snapshot proves it: fixture FACETS.seam is `{ ISP: 2, internet: 1 }` (fixtures.ts:92) — two buckets — and the snapshot renders '3 scored seams'. It is doubly wrong: the backend facet is a terms aggregation over FieldSeamType (query.go:395 `"seam": terms(FieldSeamType)`), so even the key count would be scored seam TYPES, not seams. rc1_blocking as customer-visible correctness on the security surface: the number is silently wrong (unlike 3.3-11 the reader has nothing on screen to contradict it), it inflates apparent assessment coverage, and it violates the page's own stated contract that it 'never renders a total it was not given' (SecurityOverview.tsx:40-42). The snapshot baking the wrong value means the regression test currently defends the bug.

where: src/frontend/src/pages/security/SecurityOverview.tsx:243-259 (lane cards), with the row source at :185-188 and the fetch at :139-141
rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e, and the trigger is BROADER than filed. The badge is the server-side facet `facets.evidence_class[lane]`, while the body is `topExposures(findings.filter(...))` over the first 100 findings only (`api.securityFindings({ ...q, limit: 100 })`). Two independent ways to get '12 current' over 'No verdicts yet.': (a) the pagination case the row names — more than 100 current findings, none of the lane's in the first page; and (b) the far commoner one the row misses — topExposures keeps only fail/warn verdicts (model.ts:610-616 `.filter((f) => verdictOf(f) === "fail" || verdictOf(f) === "warn")`), so ANY lane whose current findings are all passes shows its full count above an empty body, no pagination needed. That is the normal state of a healthy estate. rc1_blocking because the empty text is not merely blank: the card renders 'No verdicts yet.' and links the authored explanation sec.lane-no-producer, which states 'An empty lane means no producer reported into it... It is not a statement that the lane is clean' and points the reader at the Security lane health panel. So a lane that is working and clean is presented as a producer outage — a misleading security result that sends an operator to troubleshoot something that is not broken. Kept at low because it is UI-only and the contradicting count is on the same card, but it should not ship as-is.

rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e (fabric.go untouched since the review). `^set / system aaa authentication \S+ password\s+[^$\s]` allows exactly ONE token between 'authentication' and 'password', which matches only the two built-in leaves — `admin-user` and `linuxadmin-user` (both are what every test and every captured config in the repo use). A configured list user is `set / system aaa authentication user <name> password <value>` — TWO tokens — and the repo itself documents that spelling as legal and field-observed in another subsystem, so this is not a hypothesised syntax. The detector is bound to the `local-user-weak-secret` compliance control, and on no match it returns Tripped:false with the evidence string 'all locally stored passwords carry a `$scheme$` hash marker' — a positive assurance over a user population it structurally never examined. rc1_blocking as a misleading security result: a compliance control returns a clean verdict and its own evidence over-claims coverage. Kept at LOW rather than raised, for one mitigating fact I verified: SR Linux hashes on commit (packs.go:144 remediation says so), so a running config normally renders `$y$...` for every user and the practical false-clean window is a candidate/offline/templated config rather than a live device. The evidence string is wrong in every case, though, not just the tripping one.
evidence: fabric.go:175 `reSRLWeakPassword = regexp.MustCompile(`^set / system aaa authentication \S+ password\s+[^$\s]`)`. fabric.go:244 `return hardening.DetectResult{Tripped: false, Evidence: "all locally stored passwords carry a `$scheme$` hash marker"}`. The two-token user form is documented in this repo: src/backend/internal/threatlane/catalog.go:281 `//	set / system aaa authentication user bob …   (bare slash, space-separated — the `info … flat` / commit form)` and exercised at catalog_test.go:100 `set /system aaa authentication user backdoor password $y$j9T$`. Every fabric_test.go / testdata line uses only admin-user or linuxadmin-user (fabric_test.go:379,459,463; testdata/srlinux_spine1_running.txt:553-555) — the test corpus never contains a list user, which is why the gap survived.
suggested_fix: Widen the pattern to both shapes — e.g. `^set / system aaa authentication (?:user \S+|\S+-user) password\s+[^$\s]` — add a list-user case to fabric_test.go and to the SR Linux testdata, and make the clean evidence name what was actually examined rather than claiming all stored passwords.

where: src/backend/internal/parsetrace/parsetrace.go:180-193 (Match) and 236-256 (MarkerIn); reached from src/backend/collectors/parsehook.go:44-56 via snmptrap.go:1201
rationale: The mechanism is real but two of the row's three premises are answered in the code, and its parenthetical is factually wrong. (1) 'No arm requirement / no check that the platform minted it' is DELIBERATE and documented as the design's reason 1 — the package doc explains that requiring an arm first would make a trace's parser stage depend on a second call and produce an empty parser.log that 'would read as "the parser never saw it"'. (2) 'No rate limit' understates the containment: the sink is a ring bounded in three dimensions on purpose (1000 lines total, 200 per marker, 64 markers) with an explicit §9 rationale, and the second sink, applog.Debug, is suppressed unless the process is at debug level (applog.go:141-146), so the default-level cost of a forged marker is one bounded in-memory append and nothing durable. (3) 'Feature-flagged off by default' is NOT true at 9d981e5e — I found no flag: the ring, the sink and the parse hook are wired unconditionally in newServer (main.go:1473-1499) and the routes are registered unconditionally (main.go:3283-3287). What genuinely remains: an attacker with UDP/162 reach can mint distinct well-formed cx_debug tokens and, via evictOldestMarkerLocked, push an operator's in-flight trace markers out of the 64-marker ring, so that trace's parser/api stage reads VerdictNotSeen. That is a debug-tool degradation requiring an adversary who has trap-port reach, knows the marker format, and acts during an active trace; it destroys no telemetry, crosses no tenant boundary, and consumes no unbounded resource. Real, low value, adversary-present theoretical path — hardening, not an rc1 fix. Correcting the row's flag claim is the useful output here.
evidence: parsetrace.go:16-21 (package doc): '1. IT CARRIES ITS OWN MARKER. Every record the debugger injects carries `cx_debug=<ulid>` in its text. Such a record is traced unconditionally — requiring an operator to arm a filter first would make a trace's parser stage depend on a second call that is easy to forget, and the resulting empty parser.log would read as "the parser never saw it".' · parsetrace.go:184-186 `if m := MarkerIn(text); m != "" { return m, true }` (before the armed-needle check). · pipedebug/ring.go:15-17 'It is BOUNDED in three dimensions on purpose (§9: all queues are bounded): total lines, lines per marker, and markers tracked.' with RingCapacity=1000, ringPerMarker=200, ringMaxMarkers=64 (ring.go:26-34) and ring.go:120-122 `if _, known := r.byMk[m]; !known && len(r.byMk) >= ringMaxMarkers { r.evictOldestMarkerLocked() }`. · applog.go:141-144 `func Debug(...) { if !debugEnabled.Load() { return } ... }`. · No flag: `grep -rn 'FEATURE_PIPELINE_DEBUG|pipeline_debug' src/backend --include=*.go` returns nothing; main.go:1473 `srv.debugRing = pipedebug.NewRing()` and :1493-1499 SetSink run unconditionally. · Trap side: parsehook.go:52 `marker, ok := f.Match(ev.Message)` called from snmptrap.go:1201 in forward(), i.e. after decode and independent of communityMatchesDevice (snmptrap.go:690-698), which gates only device attribution.
suggested_fix: If revisited: reserve a slice of the ring for markers the platform actually minted (pipedebug already mints and could record them), or require the marker to be known-live before an unsolicited record may claim ring space; a per-source-IP cap on trap-side trace emissions would also do it. Independently, correct the finding text — the pipeline debugger is not feature-flagged off.

rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e and contradicts the function's own contract two lines above it. The architecture rule tests only the prefix's NETWORK ADDRESS against 2000::/3, not the whole prefix, so every IPv6 prefix shorter than /3 rooted at :: (::/0, ::/1, ::/2) is classified ReasonUnallocated even though it wholly contains the delegated global-unicast range. The IPv4 side gets this right by accident: the static table is only consulted with `r.p.Bits() <= p.Bits()`, so 0.0.0.0/0 matches nothing and there is no v4 architecture rule to fall through to. The consequence is not cosmetic: ClassBogon maps to SevHigh (classify.go:77), so a tenant that watches ::/0 gets a HIGH incident whose summary asserts the default route 'must never appear in the global table'. The sighting path makes it likelier still - bgpWatchNoteBMPAnnounce/bgpWatchNoteFeedUpdates push every announced prefix through the same Lookup, so any BMP session or live feed carrying an IPv6 default route (an ordinary thing on an edge router) registers a permanent bogon sighting on /api/bgp/bogons for that tenant. RC1-blocking as BGP/customer-visible correctness: it manufactures a high-severity false positive from routine, legitimate routing data. Raised low -> medium for that reason.
evidence: bogon.go:189-194 (Lookup's doc): "A prefix that merely COVERS a reserved block (0.0.0.0/0 covers 10/8) is NOT reported: a default route is not a bogon announcement." bogon.go:215: `if p.Addr().Is6() && !p.Addr().Is4In6() && !v6GlobalUnicast.Contains(p.Addr())` - for ::/0 the address is `::`, Is6()=true, Is4In6()=false, and 2000::/3 does not contain `::`, so the rule fires. The static loop cannot pre-empt it: bogon.go:208 requires `r.p.Bits() <= p.Bits()`, and every v6 table row has bits >= 16 while p.Bits()==0. classify.go:77 `ClassBogon: SevHigh`; classify.go:263-272 builds the incident from Lookup with no length floor; helpers.go:49-68 parsePrefix imposes no minimum prefix length, so ::/0 enters the watchlist unhindered. No commit in d796bf7d..9d981e5e touches bogon.go (the two bgpwatch fixes, 89680bd7 and 34a4538e, touch classify.go/evaluate.go/metrics.go only).
suggested_fix: Test the whole prefix, not its base address: replace `!v6GlobalUnicast.Contains(p.Addr())` with `!p.Overlaps(v6GlobalUnicast)`. That still flags 8000::/1 and ::/3 (wholly outside global unicast) while ::/0, ::/1 and ::/2 fall through to 'not a bogon', matching the v4 behaviour and Lookup's own doc. Add a table test pinning ::/0 and 0.0.0.0/0 to the same verdict.

rationale: Reproduces. parseFullBogons returns `dropped` and silently stops at FeedMaxEntries, and RefreshFeed throws both signals away on any success: `dropped` is read only in the kept==0 branch, and the success write sets feedErr to the empty string. FeedStatus has no truncated/dropped field, so a feed that was cut at 20,000 rows, or one whose format changed such that 99% of rows failed to parse, is published to the operator as a clean refresh with a fresh feedAt - which then suppresses any refetch for the full 6h FeedTTL. The failure mode is a silently shortened bogon table, i.e. false negatives on exactly the daily unallocated-by-RIR space the feed exists to cover, presented as a healthy fetch. That is a silent failure by the repo's own §10 rule ('No silent failures allowed'), which is why I keep it rc1_blocking even at low severity; the remediation is additive and cheap. Severity stays low because the feature is default-off (FEATURE_BGP_BOGON_FEED), the embedded RFC/IANA half always stands, and the truncation half needs a non-default BGP_BOGON_FEED_URL (the shipped default is the ~4k-row v4 list; the v6 list an operator would naturally point at is far larger than 20,000 rows, so the path is reachable, not hypothetical).
evidence: bogon.go:328-336: `for _, line := range strings.Split(body, "\n") { if kept >= FeedMaxEntries { break }` - truncation is a bare break with no flag. bogon.go:316-322: `rules, kept, dropped := parseFullBogons(string(body)); if kept == 0 { ... }` then `s.feed, s.feedCount, s.feedAt, s.feedURL, s.feedErr = rules, kept, now(), rawURL, ""` - `dropped` is unreferenced on the success path and feedErr is cleared. FeedStatus (bogon.go:222-232) carries only Enabled/URL/Entries/FetchedAt/Error/Note - no truncation or drop count. bogon.go:311 `fresh := !s.feedAt.IsZero() && now().Sub(s.feedAt) < FeedTTL` with FeedTTL = 6h, so the degraded copy stands for six hours. bogon_test.go has no test naming FeedMaxEntries or truncation (only the kept==0 and feed-outage cases at lines 115 and 142). doc.go:90-92 documents BGP_BOGON_FEED_URL as an operator override.
suggested_fix: Return truncation and the drop count out of parseFullBogons into FeedStatus (`truncated bool`, `rows_dropped int`), and treat a refresh that hit FeedMaxEntries, or whose drop ratio exceeds a small threshold, as a degraded refresh: record it in feedErr (or a new Warning field) and do not let it start a fresh 6h TTL.

rationale: Reproduces. `Overlaps` is symmetric, so a row whose prefix CONTAINS the queried scope is kept exactly as if it were contained in it. The queried resource's geofeed URL is a string a third party wrote into a whois object - the file's own header calls it 'the single most attacker-influenced input on this page' - and the containment filter is one of the five stated mitigations. A published feed can therefore emit `0.0.0.0/0,KP` (or `104.0.0.0/8,KP` against a queried 104.28.0.0/16) and have it rendered to the operator as a geolocation row for the resource they asked about, which is precisely the 'claims about somebody else's address space' the code promises it cannot do. The ASN path widens it: scope is up to six announced prefixes and a single feed found on one of them, so one supernet row rides in against all six. RC1-blocking as customer-visible correctness against attacker-influenced input plus a documented invariant that is simply not enforced; severity stays low because the payload is a displayed geolocation string, not a privilege, a credential or a stored record. The existing scoped test does not catch it - it only uses a DISJOINT out-of-scope row, never a supernet, so the containment claim is untested.
evidence: geofeed.go:134-136 (ParseGeofeedCSV doc): "keeping only rows whose prefix is contained in one of `within`". geofeed.go:26-29 (trust posture): "only rows inside the queried resource are kept, so a feed cannot inject claims about somebody else's address space into this answer". geofeed.go:231: `if w.Overlaps(p) { return true }` - netip.Prefix.Overlaps is true when either prefix contains the other. geofeed_test.go:64-81 TestParseGeofeedCSVIsConservativeAndScoped uses scope 104.28.0.0/16 against realGeofeedCSV whose out-of-scope row is 103.22.200.0/24, disjoint - a supernet row would pass this test unchanged. No commit in d796bf7d..9d981e5e touches internal/bgpdepth.
suggested_fix: One line: `if w.Bits() <= p.Bits() && w.Contains(p.Addr()) { return true }`. Add a regression row to TestParseGeofeedCSVIsConservativeAndScoped: a `0.0.0.0/0,KP` line against scope 104.28.0.0/16 must be excluded (and counted as out-of-scope, not as a drop).

rationale: Reproduces as described, and the O(1) alternative really is available: the ring is append-only in seq order, so newest = buf[(head-1+n)%n].Seq and oldest = buf[(head-count+n)%n].Seq - no walk needed. Today Stats calls ring.newestFirst with a callback that always returns true, so it walks every retained record of every admitted session while holding s.mu, the same non-RW mutex every BMP connection goroutine takes to record an update (Record/Close/RecordParseError all lock it). All three read endpoints pay it, and handleUpdates pays it on top of its own ring walk. The worst case is larger than the filed 22 ms estimate: MaxSessionRecords=256 retained sessions x MaxUpdatesPerSession=4096 = ~1.05M iterations, and UpdateRecord is a ~300-byte struct passed BY VALUE to the callback, so this is a cache-miss-bound walk over a few hundred MB, and a cross-tenant reader (cross=true) walks every session in the process. Not rc1_blocking: the work is hard-bounded by construction (the ring allocates its whole backing array at open, doc.go:101-112), nothing is computed incorrectly, no data is lost or leaked by it, and the requester only ever scans sessions scopeAdmits lets them see. It is an efficiency and lock-hold defect, which the rc1 list does not cover ('uncontrolled resource exhaustion' does not fit a statically bounded scan).
evidence: store.go:849-857: `st.ring.newestFirst(func(rec UpdateRecord) bool { ... return true })` - the callback never returns false, so store.go:154-161 `for i := 0; i < r.count; i++` runs to completion for every session. store.go:826-827: `s.mu.Lock(); defer s.mu.Unlock()` around the whole loop; store.go:164-166 documents that same mutex as the one 'the listener writes from N connection goroutines' contends for. Call sites: http.go:169 (handleSessions), http.go:185 (handleStats), http.go:272 (handleUpdates). doc.go:107 MaxSessionRecords = 256, doc.go:112 MaxUpdatesPerSession = 4096. store.go:248-269 Close marks a session closed but never releases its ring, so retired sessions keep contributing to the walk.
suggested_fix: Give updateRing O(1) accessors (oldestSeq/newestSeq computed from head and count) and have Stats read those instead of newestFirst; alternatively track min/max seq on push. Either keeps the reported values identical and removes the walk from the mutex.

where: src/backend/internal/bmp/store.go:396 (s.seq++), surfaced at store.go:787 (viewOf .Seq) and http.go:277 (next_cursor)
rationale: Reproduces, and it contradicts a decision the module states in writing one function away. `s.seq` is a single process-wide counter incremented once per prefix across every session of every tenant. Its value is published verbatim in each row's `seq`, in StatsView.Oldest/NewestUpdateSeq, and inside next_cursor - which is plain base64 of the decimal, not an opaque token. A tenant that reads /api/bgp/bmp/updates twice and subtracts the newest seq, then subtracts its own contribution, learns how many BGP updates every OTHER tenant's routers produced in that interval. handleStats deliberately withholds exactly that quantity, in a comment that calls it 'another tenant's data', so this is a leak measured against the module's own stated boundary rather than an invented standard. RC1-blocking under tenant isolation: it is a metadata side channel, but it is a real, trivially exploitable one that reveals per-tenant activity volume and timing to any authenticated tenant. Severity stays low because it discloses only aggregate counters - no prefixes, peers, devices or rows of another tenant cross the boundary.
evidence: store.go:169 `seq uint64` on the process-wide Store (one instance, not per tenant); store.go:396 `s.seq++` inside `add`, executed for every announced/withdrawn prefix of every session regardless of tenant, with store.go:399 `Seq: s.seq`. store.go:787 `Seq: rec.Seq` puts it in the JSON row view. http.go:277 `body["next_cursor"] = encodeCursor(rows[len(rows)-1].Seq)` and http.go:351-353 `encodeCursor` = `base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte(cursorPrefix + strconv.FormatUint(seq, 10)))` - decodable by anyone. store.go:820-821 StatsView.OldestUpdateSeq/NewestUpdateSeq expose it again. The contradicted decision, http.go:173-175: "handleStats serves GET /api/bgp/bmp/stats - the caller's OWN aggregate. The process-wide counters are deliberately not exposed here: another tenant's message volume is another tenant's data."
suggested_fix: Either keep a per-session (or per-tenant) monotonic ordinal for the wire and use the global seq only as an internal tiebreaker, or stop publishing Seq in UpdateView and make the cursor opaque (HMAC or encrypt the {tenant, seq} pair) so the raw counter never leaves the process. Whichever is chosen, Stats' Oldest/NewestUpdateSeq must move to the same non-global scale.

rationale: Reproduces exactly as filed, and only for a whitespace-only key. validatePolicy trims into `key`, then files the empty-key error under the UNTRIMMED `row.key`, while the panel looks it up under the trimmed one. For row.key === '' the two agree ('.key') and the message renders; for row.key === '   ' the error lands at '   .key' and the panel reads '.key', finds nothing, and shows nothing - while save() has already returned early because the error map is non-empty. The operator gets no message, no 'Saved.', and a Save button that stays enabled, so the form is a dead end until they clear the field. Not rc1_blocking: nothing is written, nothing is lost or corrupted, no false success is shown (the absence of 'Saved.' is honest), no boundary is crossed, and the workaround is to empty or fix the field. It is form-plumbing correctness with a one-line fix, which the rc1 list treats as non-blocking. Severity stays low. Note that 89680bd7 (in the post-review window) did touch bgpAlerts.model.ts, but only emptySetConsequence/policy-note text - the validate/render key mismatch is untouched at 9d981e5e.
evidence: bgpAlerts.model.ts:388-392: `const key = row.key.trim(); if (key === "") { errs[`${row.key}.key`] = "A per-prefix policy needs the prefix it applies to."; continue; }` - note `row.key`, not `key`. AlertPolicyPanel.tsx:284: `<FieldError msg={errs[`${row.key.trim()}.key`]} />`. AlertPolicyPanel.tsx:183-185: `const v = validatePolicy(form, limits); setErrs(v); if (Object.keys(v).length > 0) return;` - the early return with no aggregate banner (`err` at AlertPolicyPanel.tsx:227 is set only from API rejections at lines 169 and 198). Every other branch of validatePolicy files under the trimmed `key` (lines 394, 398), so this is the single inconsistent site.
suggested_fix: File the empty-key error under the trimmed key: `errs[`${key}.key`]` (or key rows by index, which also fixes the duplicate-blank-row collision). Add a bgpAlerts.model.test.ts case asserting validatePolicy('   ') produces an entry at '.key'.

where: src/frontend/src/pages/bgp/{RpkiPanel.tsx:41, AspaCard.tsx:31, BogonsPanel.tsx:80, GeofeedPanel.tsx:37, AsPathGraphPanel.tsx:96, PeersPanel.tsx:74} and components/rca/RcaVerdictFeedback.tsx:38-42
rationale: Reproduces. All six BGP panels render `e.message || "<fallback>"`, and api.ts throws the raw envelope `Error("<status> <statusText>: <body>")`, so the server's wrap chain - internal service names, container hostnames and 172.18.x.x addresses - reaches the operator's screen verbatim. Not rc1_blocking: the viewer is already authenticated and authorized for the page, no credential or secret transits the path (the leaked strings are internal hostnames and dial errors, which errors.ts classifies as 'infrastructure disclosure', not secrets), no data is lost or mis-stated, and no tenant boundary is crossed. RpkiPanel.tsx:41 `.catch((e: Error) => { if (alive) setErr(e.message || "RPKI lookup failed"); })`, and the identical shape at AspaCard.tsx:31, BogonsPanel.tsx:80, GeofeedPanel.tsx:37, AsPathGraphPanel.tsx:96, PeersPanel.tsx:74. RcaVerdictFeedback.tsx:38-42: `const detail = msg.replace(/^\d{3}\s*[^:]*:\s*/, "").trim(); return detail ? `Could not record the verdict: ${detail}` : ...` - no developer-text filter. lib/errors.ts header: "what actually reached the screen was: 500 Internal Server Error: {\"error\":\"clickhouse: dial tcp 172.18.0.9:9000: connect: connection refused\"} ... it leaks internal hostnames and component names into the product", and looksLikeDeveloperText already rejects IP:port, host:port and dial/EOF/connection-refused vocabulary. A lint rule or a test asserting no BGP panel renders a string matching the envelope regex would keep it from recurring.

rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e and is the exact twin, in the peer lane, of the defect the branch already fixed for prefixes in 34a4538e ("a failed lookup no longer closes a live hijack"). checkPeers collapses the tri-state to a boolean: `down := strings.EqualFold(strings.TrimSpace(p.State), "down")`, so State=="unknown" is treated as UP. bmp.Store.Close sets `p.seen = false` for every peer of a closed session, and sessionState.view() renders `State: "unknown"` when !p.seen — the store's own comment says "every peer's state is now UNKNOWN rather than up. Reporting a stale 'up' after the feed died is exactly the comfortable lie this module exists not to tell." bgpWatchPeers copies that State verbatim into PeerObservation (`State: p.State`), and Store.Sessions() returns CLOSED sessions too, so the peer does not vanish and the correctly-handled vanished-peer branch is never reached. Result: the moment a BMP session drops (router reload, TCP reset — routine), every peer that was legitimately down is dispatched as Alert{Resolved:true, "BGP peer X on Y is back up."} and its down-state is deleted, while the peer is in fact still down and we have simply stopped measuring. Raised medium→high: this is a false RESOLUTION of a live incident on the operator's pager, fires on an ordinary event rather than a hostile one, and the codebase's own ClassUnknown fix (evaluate.go:462-476) declares this class of behaviour unacceptable. No test pins the current behaviour — evaluate_test.go:249 only exercises an explicit State "up", and the vanish test at :260 covers the other branch.
evidence: evaluate.go:534 `down := strings.EqualFold(strings.TrimSpace(p.State), "down")`; store.go Close(): `p.up = false; p.seen = false` with comment "every peer's state is now UNKNOWN rather than up"; store.go view(): `State: "unknown"` then `if p.seen { pv.State = "down"; if p.up { pv.State = "up" } }`; PeerObservation doc `State string // up | down | unknown`; Store.Sessions() has no closed-session filter.
suggested_fix: Treat only an explicitly measured "up" as a recovery: derive a tri-state (up/down/unknown) and, on unknown, KEEP st.peerDown and emit no Resolve — mirroring applyIncident's ClassUnknown branch (optionally a bgp_measurement_lost-style notice for peers).

rationale: Reproduces. The peer recovery branch calls e.deps.Resolve(...) and bumps alerts_resolved_total but never touches st.cooldown, while the two other places that end an episode both clear it: resolveAlert does `delete(st.cooldown, key)` with the comment "The episode is over, so both its stamps go", and ForgetPrefix does `delete(st.cooldown, alertKey(t, key, class))` because (evaluate.go:810) "otherwise re-adding the prefix inside the window silently suppresses". The peer alert id "bgp:<tenant>:peer:<device>|<peer>" therefore keeps a stamp for the full 60-minute cool-down after a resolve was already sent. A peer that flaps down again inside that window hits `if !e.coolDownPassed(...)` → bump alerts_suppressed_total → return, so there is NO notification, NO recorded alert AND no evidence record (the EventFromPeerDown call sits inside the suppressed branch), even though the operator was explicitly told the peer came back up. That is a silent loss of a delivered-and-then-retracted signal plus durable evidence, not mere dampening — the cool-down is documented as a per-episode floor, and the episode ended at the resolve. Not a duplicate of 3.4-01: distinct defect (missing cool-down clear) in the same function, and it bites even on a correctly measured down→up→down.
evidence: resolveAlert: `delete(st.cooldown, key)` / "The episode is over, so both its stamps go"; ForgetPrefix comment evaluate.go:810 "cooldown for that prefix CLEARED — otherwise re-adding the prefix inside"; peer recovery branch contains only Resolve(...) + e.bump(st, "alerts_resolved_total", ...) — grep of `cooldown` in bgpwatch shows deletes only at evaluate.go:701, 704, 855, none on a peer key.
suggested_fix: In the `!down && wasDown` branch, `delete(st.cooldown, "bgp:"+tenant+":peer:"+key)` under e.mu, exactly as resolveAlert does — and only when the recovery is a MEASURED "up" (see 3.4-01).

rationale: Reproduces, and the package's own documentation condemns it. ParseBGPState uses the boolean shim ParseASNValue and, on a miss, `continue`s — splicing the surviving hops into one path. ParseASNValue's own doc (aspa.go:265) says "A caller that must REPORT a broken source (rather than silently shortening a list) uses parseASNValue and its three states directly", and asnParse's doc says collapsing asnUnreadable with asnReserved "reports a broken upstream as a shorter list (CLAUDE.md §10)". The sibling parseASPathString does exactly the right thing — it appends `unreadableHop` (AS0, RFC 7607) so BuildASPathGraph counts PathsDropped and refuses the path, and aspath_test.go:201/209 pin that ("a fabricated adjacency 6939→3333 was drawn across an unreadable hop"). bgp-state is the PRIMARY source (bgp_ops.go:960-968 tries bgp-state first, looking-glass only when it yields nothing), so the fabricated-adjacency guard is absent on the path almost every request takes. Reachable with a realistic payload: an AS_SET rendered as "{1299,1300}" inside the integer path array parses as unreadable, is dropped, and 7018→3333 is drawn as an adjacency while PathsDropped stays 0 and the panel reports full coverage. BGP correctness + silent misreporting of coverage → rc1 blocking. Severity held at medium: it needs a malformed/unusual upstream element, and the blast radius is a wrong edge in the AS-path graph, not an alert or a deletion.

where: src/backend/internal/bgpdepth/aspa.go:156 (HTTPProvider.ASPA) → src/backend/bgp_ops.go:863 handleBGPASPA; leak origin src/backend/bgp_ops.go:762
rationale: Reproduces end to end. bgpFetcher.Get returns the transport error verbatim (`resp, err := f.webClient.Do(req); if err != nil { return nil, err }`), which for any dial/TLS/timeout failure is a *url.Error whose Error() renders the FULL request URL — and ASPA composes that URL from the operator-configured Base with its query preserved (`q := u.Query(); q.Set("asn", ...); u.RawQuery = q.Encode()`), so a token in BGP_ASPA_PROVIDER_URL's query string is inside the string. aspa.go:156 wraps it with %w, and handleBGPASPA puts it in a 200 body TWICE (`st.Reason = "The configured ASPA provider did not answer: " + err.Error()` and `out["error"] = err.Error()`) behind only requirePerm("infrastructure", LevelRead) — a per-tenant read permission, while the provider URL is platform-global config. The package explicitly anticipates this exact secret: ASPAStatus.Host is documented "the configured provider's HOSTNAME only — never the full URL, which may carry a token (§8: no secrets in responses or logs)", and aspaBaseHost exists solely for that. SafeOutboundURL rejects userinfo but says nothing about query credentials. Credentials/secrets + privilege boundary → rc1 blocking. Held at medium: it needs the operator to have put a token in the URL query (the HowTo text points at Routinator/rpki-client, usually unauthenticated) and an upstream transport failure.
evidence: bgp_ops.go:760-763 `resp, err := f.webClient.Do(req); if err != nil { return nil, err }`; aspa.go:154-157 `body, err := p.F.Get(ctx, u.String(), ASPARespCap) ... fmt.Errorf("aspa provider: %w", err)`; handleBGPASPA `st.Reason = "The configured ASPA provider did not answer: " + err.Error()` and `out["error"] = err.Error()` then `writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, out)`; ASPAStatus.Host doc "never the full URL, which may carry a token".
suggested_fix: Sanitize at the boundary: in HTTPProvider.ASPA replace the transport error with a host-only message (aspaBaseHost(p.Base) + a classified reason), or have bgpFetcher.Get strip *url.Error's URL (return a `url.Error`-free error naming only the hostname). Belt-and-braces: have handleBGPASPA emit a fixed reason and log the detail scrubbed.

rationale: Reproduces, and the documented premise of the exemption is factually wrong. The comment justifies skipping the post-DNS gate because "when an egress proxy is configured, the dial target IS the proxy" — but the transport is `http.ProxyFromEnvironment`, and Go's httpproxy.FromEnvironment reads only HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/NO_PROXY (verified in GOROOT src/vendor/golang.org/x/net/http/httpproxy/proxy.go: `HTTPSProxy: getEnvAny("HTTPS_PROXY", "https_proxy")`; no ALL_PROXY anywhere in that file). With ALL_PROXY/all_proxy set and HTTPS_PROXY unset, `proxied` is true, d.Control is never installed, and the request is dialled DIRECT with no address check — the second, "non-optional half" of the SSRF gate (CheckDialAddress, whose own doc says "a hostname that resolves to 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata) or 10.x is stopped even though the URL looked fine") is silently off. SafeOutboundURL only screens literal-IP hosts (`if addr, err := netip.ParseAddr(host); err == nil && !publicAddr(addr)`), so a hostname resolving internally passes. This client is the one pointed at URLs discovered in UNTRUSTED registry data (geofeeds from whois remarks) plus the operator ASPA URL, so an attacker-published geofeed URL reaches cloud metadata / internal admin ports. ALL_PROXY is a common shell convention (curl, many container images set it alongside or instead of HTTPS_PROXY), so this is a plausible deployment, not a contrived one. No test or doc anywhere else in the repo references ALL_PROXY — the only other hit is the review document itself.
evidence: bgp_ops.go:316-317 `proxied := os.Getenv("HTTPS_PROXY") != "" || os.Getenv("https_proxy") != "" || os.Getenv("ALL_PROXY") != "" || os.Getenv("all_proxy") != ""` then `if !proxied { d.Control = ... CheckDialAddress }`; GOROOT httpproxy/proxy.go line 83 "environment variables HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY" — no ALL_PROXY; fetch.go CheckDialAddress doc "the second — and non-optional — half of the SSRF gate".
suggested_fix: Decide the exemption from the transport, not from raw env: keep d.Control ALWAYS installed and instead ask `http.ProxyFromEnvironment(req)` per request (or precompute httpproxy.FromEnvironment().ProxyFunc()) — skip the address check only for a request that actually resolves to a proxy URL. At minimum drop ALL_PROXY/all_proxy from the `proxied` test, and account for NO_PROXY matching the target.

rationale: Reproduces on both lenses. (a) The retry branch is dead: it fires only on `errors.As(aerr, &ne) && ne.Timeout()`, and Accept returns a timeout only when a deadline was set — grep for SetDeadline in the package finds only per-connection SetReadDeadline (listener.go:243, 277), never on the listener. (b) Any other accept error is terminal: one LogWarn then `return`, and the deferred shutdown() closes the listener. Go's netFD.accept retries EINTR/EAGAIN/ECONNABORTED internally, so what actually escapes is fd exhaustion (EMFILE/ENFILE) — realistic on a shared api process — and it kills the BMP receiver for the LIFE OF THE PROCESS: API.Run just calls listener.Run once, main.go starts it as `workers.start("bmp-receiver", …)` with no restart supervision, and there is no re-bind path. Meanwhile the read surface keeps asserting `coverage{Receiver: true, …}` (hardcoded, doc: "always true where these routes are registered") and, with sessions gone, prints "No router is exporting BMP to this platform. This is an empty FEED … point a router's BMP export at the receiver" — i.e. it blames the operator's router for a dead socket. Durable telemetry loss + a misleading status that survives until restart is exactly the silent-failure class CLAUDE.md's monitoring section and the package's own doc ("no failure path is silent") exist to prevent. Held at medium: it needs an fd-exhaustion-class event, and one warning line is logged.
evidence: listener.go:105-113 `var ne net.Error; if errors.As(aerr, &ne) && ne.Timeout() { … time.After(AcceptBackoff); continue }` followed by `l.deps.LogWarn("BMP accept failed", …); return`; `defer shutdown()` closes ln on that return; no SetDeadline on ln anywhere in the package; bmp.go:157 `func (a *API) Run(ctx) { … a.listener.Run(ctx) }` (one shot); http.go:128 `c := coverage{Receiver: true, …}`.
suggested_fix: Retry on any non-fatal accept error with the existing AcceptBackoff (bounded, e.g. exponential up to ~1s, as net/http.Server.Serve does), reserving the terminal return for a closed listener; surface a real liveness fact (listener bound / last accept error) in coverage instead of the hardcoded Receiver:true, and count accept failures in Metrics so the watchdog can see it.

rationale: Reproduces verbatim at 9d981e5e. FileStore.SetGolden mutates rows[i].Golden=false in place while scanning (rows is the live slice from s.rows[k], so the writes land in the register), and only decides afterwards whether the requested sha existed. A 404 therefore leaves the device with NO golden baseline. The 404 is reachable for three distinct inputs: an unknown sha, a pruned sha, and — the nastiest — a FAILED capture row, because failureSHA() (manager.go:568) is a real SHA256 hex so it passes the handler's validSHA() gate at http.go:313, reaches the store, and is then rejected inside the loop by the `rows[i].Status == StatusOK` condition. The consequence is worse than a lost UI flag: retentionSplit() protects the golden row from pruning by testing `case v.Golden:`, so once the mark is silently cleared the baseline row and its sealed blob become prunable, and every subsequent drift verdict has no reference to compare against. The Postgres backend is correct — its SetGolden returns ErrNotFound from inside db.WithTenant, and platformdb/db.go:333 `defer func() { _ = tx.Rollback(ctx) }()` undoes the clear — so the two backends disagree about the same operation. Untouched by the 27 post-review commits.
evidence: store.go:259-268: `for i := range rows { switch { case rows[i].SHA == sha && rows[i].Status == StatusOK: rows[i].Golden = true; found = true; default: rows[i].Golden = false } } ... if !found { return ErrNotFound }` — the default arm has already run on every row before the found check. manager.go:545 `SHA: failureSHA(dev.ID, now)`; manager.go:568-570 `return SHA256Hex("capture-failure\x00" + deviceID ...)`. store.go:92 `case v.Golden: kept = append(kept, v)` is the only thing keeping the baseline out of `doomed`. `git diff d796bf7d..9d981e5e -- .../configstore/store.go` shows only retentionSplit/Prune changes; SetGolden is unmodified.
suggested_fix: Locate the target row (and confirm Status==StatusOK) in a first pass, return ErrNotFound before mutating anything, then clear-and-set in a second pass — mirroring the pgStore ordering. A cheaper variant: snapshot the previous golden (tenant,sha) and restore it on the !found path before returning.

rationale: Reproduces. Same family as 3.5-01 but a different function and a different trigger, so not a duplicate. insertLocked does `s.rows[k][i] = v` — a wholesale replacement — and the Version the capture path builds at manager.go:422-425 never sets Golden, so it is false. The trigger is precisely the rollback-to-baseline workflow the product exists to support: a device is reverted to its golden configuration and the next capture hashes to the golden sha. Because that sha differs from prev.SHA (the golden is an OLDER version than Latest), the capture takes the else branch at manager.go:437, mints a fresh Version, and Store.Put overwrites the golden row with Golden=false. The 'unchanged' branch is safe only by accident (`ver = prev` carries prev.Golden forward when the golden happens to also be the latest). Once the flag is gone, retentionSplit no longer shields the row, so the baseline and its sealed blob can be deleted by the very next prune — state corruption escalating to data loss. Postgres is again correct and again divergent: the ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE column list at store.go:441-447 omits `golden`, so the flag survives.
evidence: store.go:156-160: `for i, existing := range s.rows[k] { if existing.SHA == v.SHA { s.rows[k][i] = v; return } }`. manager.go:422-425 builds `ver := Version{... Status: StatusOK, Drift: DriftUnknown}` with no Golden field. manager.go:437-451 else-branch: `outcome = OutcomeNew ... if err := m.deps.Store.Put(ctx, tenant, false, ver); err != nil`. pg contrast, store.go:441-447: `ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, device_id, version_sha) DO UPDATE SET captured_at=..., size_bytes=..., blob_ref=..., vendor=..., status=..., error_text=...` — golden deliberately absent. No test asserts golden survives a re-Put; store_test.go only covers SetGolden singularity and cross-tenant refusal.
suggested_fix: In insertLocked, preserve owner-set fields the caller did not compute — carry `existing.Golden` (and arguably existing.Drift/Added/Removed, which Put also blanks) onto v before the assignment, so the file backend matches the Postgres ON CONFLICT column list exactly.

rationale: Reproduces. The MTU/BW/speed/duplex scan sits AFTER the switch and outside it, with no `continue` on the description arm, so it runs over every line of the record including `Description:`. All four writes are first-write-wins (`if cur.MTU == nil`, `if cur.SpeedMbps == nil`, `if cur.SpeedMbps == nil || cur.Duplex == nil`), and in real Cisco-family `show interfaces` output the description line PRECEDES the MTU/BW line and the duplex/speed line — the repo's own fixture proves the ordering. So a description wins over the device's real values, not the other way round. Concretely: `Description: jumbo MTU 9000 to core` → numberAfter(fs,"MTU") returns 9000 and cur.MTU is pinned before the genuine `MTU 1500 bytes` line is read; `Description: 1Gbps uplink` → speedTokenMbps("1gbps") returns 1000 via the gbps arm at helpers.go:421; `Description: Full-duplex circuit` → ciscoDuplexSpeed sets Duplex. The fixture uses the benign `Description: uplink to core-02`, which contains no digits and no speed token — a textbook double that cannot catch this. These fields feed InterfaceState into protocoldiag's typed bridge and from there into RCA findings and LLM evidence, so the parser reports a value the device never printed for that field, which the package header says is the exact class it exists to prevent. e818c60d hardened the sentinel sites but did not touch this block.

Fixture ordering, fixtures_test.go:18-26: header, Hardware line, `Description: uplink to core-02` (line 20), `MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec` (line 22), `Full Duplex, 1000Mbps` (line 26).
suggested_fix: Add `continue` to the description arm of the switch (and to any other arm whose line is free text), or gate the position-independent block on `!strings.HasPrefix(trim(low), "description:")`. The Junos/VRP/SROS parsers already CutPrefix-and-continue on their description lines, so this brings the Cisco parser into line with its siblings.

where: NetOps_Observability/src/backend/internal/pcap/manager.go:418 (run success path) and :447 (fail), against the ctx built at manager.go:346
rationale: Reproduces on the Postgres backend. run() builds one context with `total = duration + StopGrace + 2*StopGrace` and uses it for BOTH the device work and the terminal metadata write. The whole purpose of that deadline is to fire when the device stops answering — and when it fires, m.fail(ctx, ...) calls Store.Put with an already-expired context. pcap's pgStore.Put passes ctx straight to db.WithTenant and tx.Exec, so pgx refuses immediately: the capture is never marked failed and the row stays StatusRunning forever in the operator's list. The file backend hides this entirely (`func (s *FileStore) Put(_ context.Context, ...)` ignores ctx), which is why no test catches it — and Postgres is now the default store for fresh installs. The success path carries the sharper edge: the fetch can complete just inside the deadline and the ctx expire before line 418, in which case the Put fails and the error handler at 420-427 DELETES the sealed blob it just wrote, destroying a capture that actually succeeded. The module already knows the right pattern and applies it one function away — cleanup() at manager.go:466-470 builds `context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), StopGrace)` precisely so a cancelled capture still finishes its work. Untouched by 39d6246f, which only added the StatusStored guard in prune() and (using the same expired ctx, though harmlessly) a prune call in fail().
evidence: manager.go:343-347: `total := time.Duration(bounds.DurationSec)*time.Second + StopGrace + 2*StopGrace; ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), total)`. manager.go:418 `if err := m.deps.Store.Put(ctx, scope.Tenant, scope.Cross, rec); err != nil {` followed by 422-426 `if derr := m.deps.Blobs.Delete(ref); derr != nil`. manager.go:447 `if err := m.deps.Store.Put(ctx, scope.Tenant, scope.Cross, rec); err != nil { m.deps.LogError("failed packet capture could not be recorded" ...) }`. pcap/store.go:413-421 pgStore.Put → `p.db.WithTenant(ctx, ...)` → `tx.Exec(ctx, ...)`; pcap/store.go:251 `func (s *FileStore) Put(_ context.Context, ...)` — the ctx is discarded, so the file-backed tests can never fail here. Contrast manager.go:466-470 cleanup(): `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), StopGrace)`.
suggested_fix: Give the terminal metadata writes their own short context derived from context.Background() (the cleanup() idiom): a `writeCtx` used by fail(), by the success-path Store.Put, and by prune(). The device ctx should bound only Gateway.Exec/Fetch.

rationale: Reproduces, and it is a direct violation of a written repo rule rather than a style preference: CLAUDE.md §9 RELIABILITY RULES states 'All network calls must retry with backoff + jitter'. There is no retry anywhere on this path — grep for retry/backoff across internal/configstore returns only the word 'attempt' in a metrics comment and in the failureSHA comment. The cost is concrete, not theoretical: DefaultInterval is 24 hours (doc.go:81), so a single TCP reset or a device that drops one SSH connection costs a full day of configuration history, writes a StatusFailed row, and fires deps.OnFailure — an operator-visible false alarm for a device that is perfectly healthy. The budget is comfortable: DefaultCaptureTimeout is 60s end to end with a 10s DefaultDialTimeout (doc.go:92-94), so two or three attempts fit inside the existing bound, and the operation is an idempotent read-only `show running-config`, so a retry is safe by construction. Not DEFERRED_HARDENING: a mid-session TCP reset to a network device is an everyday event, not a theoretical path. Not rc1_blocking, though: nothing is lost or corrupted, the failure is recorded truthfully rather than silently, the next scheduled pass recovers on its own, and an on-demand capture is available meanwhile — this is reliability polish, not a correctness or data-integrity defect.
evidence: sshgw.go:145-148 `conn, err := dial(ctx, "tcp", addr); if err != nil { return "", fmt.Errorf("connect: %w", err) }` — single shot, returns. sshgw.go:163-166 `sshConn, chans, reqs, err := ssh.NewClientConn(conn, addr, cfg); if err != nil { _ = conn.Close(); return "", fmt.Errorf("ssh handshake: %w", err) }` — single shot. sshgw.go:178 `if err := session.Run(command); err != nil` — single shot. `grep -rn 'retry|Retry|backoff|Backoff|attempt' internal/configstore/*.go` (non-test) yields only manager.go:278/543 and metrics.go:52/121 comments. doc.go:81 `DefaultInterval = 24 * time.Hour`; doc.go:92-94 `DefaultCaptureTimeout = 60 * time.Second`, `DefaultDialTimeout = 10 * time.Second`.
suggested_fix: Wrap dial+handshake+session in a bounded retry (2-3 attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, capped by the remaining ctx deadline). Retry only transient classes — dial errors, EOF/reset during handshake — and never a host-key mismatch, an auth failure, ErrTooLarge, or a non-zero command exit, all of which are deterministic and must fail on the first attempt.

rationale: Reproduces exactly as filed, and I am raising it from low to medium because the broken case is the COMMON case, not an edge. Junos borrows FreeBSD's uptime line, which prints the singular 'user' whenever exactly one session is open — and one session is the normal state during a collection, since the collector's own SSH login is usually the only one. Traced by hand: for `10:00AM  up 10 days,  2:31, 1 user, load averages: 0.10, 0.15, 0.20`, valueAfter(t," up ") returns everything from `10 days,` onward; `strings.Cut(v, " users")` finds no separator so head is the ENTIRE remainder (Cut returns before=s when sep is absent); the trailing-comma trim is a no-op because the string ends in `0.20`; the fields()-drop-last then removes only the final load figure. Result: Uptime = `10 days, 2:31, 1 user, load averages: 0.10, 0.15`. With two or more users the same trace yields the correct `10 days, 2:31`. This is squarely the documented test-double pattern the brief warns about — the fixture at fixtures_test.go:448 writes `1 users`, a string FreeBSD/Junos can never print, so the only tested single-session case is a fabricated one and the shipped path is uncovered. rc1_blocking because Uptime is customer-visible platform-health evidence: 'did this device reboot?' is a first-order RCA question, and the field feeds LLM evidence as a string that now silently carries load averages instead of an elapsed time.
evidence: platform.go:316-326: `if ph.Uptime == nil && hasFold(t, "load averages") { if v, ok := valueAfter(t, " up "); ok { head, _, _ := strings.Cut(v, " users") ... if fs := fields(head); len(fs) > 1 { head = trim(strings.TrimSuffix(strings.Join(fs[:len(fs)-1], " "), ",")) } ...` — the only user-count stripper is the literal " users". helpers.go:345-359 valueAfter returns trim(line[end:]), i.e. the whole tail. fixtures_test.go:448: `10:00AM  up 10 days,  2:31, 1 users, load averages: 0.10, 0.15, 0.20` — the impossible plural is what makes the test pass.
suggested_fix: Cut on the load-average marker instead of the user count — take everything before "load averages" (or before ", N user"/", N users" via a small match that accepts both spellings) and then strip the trailing user clause. A fixture pair covering both `1 user` and `2 users` should land with the fix; the existing `1 users` fixture must be corrected, since it currently certifies output no device produces.

where: NetOps_Observability/src/backend/internal/showparse/bgp.go:120-124 (bgpRowHead), reached via the DialectCiscoIOSXR registration at bgp.go:21-22
rationale: Reproduces, and I am raising it from low to medium because 'fails closed to the regex analyzer' understates the consequence. bgpRowHead demands `ver >= 4 && ver <= 6` in column 1. parseCiscoBGPSummary is registered for DialectCiscoIOSXR, and statebattery.go:502 sends IOS-XR the command `show bgp summary` — whose header is `Neighbor Spk AS MsgRcvd MsgSent TblVer InQ OutQ Up/Down St/PfxRcd`. Column 1 on XR is the speaker id (0 on a single-speaker box, small integers on a distributed one), never the BGP version, so `atoiOK` succeeds and the range test then rejects every row. The typed binding is therefore dead for the whole IOS-XR platform. What matters is what runs instead: typedBGPPeers returns ok=false, so analyze.go falls back to the regex matchers — and the code comments there state plainly that the typed path exists BECAUSE those regexes are false-positive prone ('the word "Idle" appearing anywhere ELSE in the output — a description, a log echo, another column — can no longer fire this verdict'; '"active" is an ordinary English word that appears in plenty of BGP output'). The fallbacks are `(?i)\bidle\b` and `(?i)\b(active|connect)\b` matched against the entire captured output, and IOS-XR's `show bgp summary` preamble is exactly the kind of text that trips them (it prints a `BGP table state: Active` header line on a healthy speaker). So the platform that gets no typed protection is also the platform whose output most invites a false tell, and the resulting verdict is emitted at ConfidenceHigh. That is BGP/RCA correctness, hence rc1_blocking. This is a defect, not a FEATURE_GAP: the parser is explicitly registered for XR and its doc comment claims 'IOS / IOS-XE / IOS-XR / NX-OS summary row', so it fails against stated behaviour. Corroborating the never-validated claim: the repo contains no IOS-XR BGP summary sample at all — showparse_test.go covers IOSXE, EOS, Junos, SROS and VRP but never IOSXR, and grep for 'Spk ' or 'BGP table state' across the whole tree returns nothing.
evidence: bgp.go:118-124: `ver, verOK := atoiOK(fs[1]); if !verOK || ver < 4 || ver > 6 { return "", 0, false }`. bgp.go:21-22 registers parseCiscoBGPSummary for `DialectCiscoIOSXR`. protocoldiag/statebattery.go:502 `showparse.DialectCiscoIOSXR: "show bgp summary"` (vs `show ip bgp summary` for IOS/IOS-XE/NX-OS/EOS). typedbridge.go:66-68 `if err != nil || res.Skipped || len(res.BGPPeers) == 0 { return nil, false }`. analyze.go:200-201 `reBgpIdle := regexp.MustCompile("(?i)\\bidle\\b")`, `reBgpActiveConnect := regexp.MustCompile("(?i)\\b(active|connect)\\b")`; analyze.go:397-410 the bgp-tcp-blocked rule with `Confidence: ConfidenceHigh` takes that regex whenever `!typed`. No IOSXR case in showparse_test.go:727-780; `grep -rn 'BGP table state|Spk ' .` over the worktree returns nothing.
suggested_fix: Bind IOS-XR to its own parser (or relax bgpRowHead behind a dialect-aware head validator) that reads column 1 as a speaker id rather than a BGP version, keeping the closed state-word set and the folded St/PfxRcd handling unchanged. Ship it with a real `show bgp summary` XR fixture including the multi-line preamble, and add a regression asserting the typed path — not the regex fallback — is what answers for DialectCiscoIOSXR.

rationale: Real and unchanged at 9d981e5e (`git log d796bf7d..9d981e5e -- src/backend/internal/showparse/logs.go` is empty). parseCiscoSyslog is registered for DialectCiscoIOSXR (logs.go:21-22) and the state battery really does collect XR logs (`statebattery.go:606: showparse.DialectCiscoIOSXR: "show logging last "+logLines`). IOS-XR's grammar is %<group>-<subgroup>-<severity>-<code>, four parts. Trace for `RP/0/RSP0/CPU0:Sep 2 09:58:12.345 UTC: %PKT_INFRA-LINK-3-UPDOWN : Interface Gi0/0/0/0, changed state to Down`: rest="PKT_INFRA-LINK-3-UPDOWN : Interface…", Cut(": ") -> tag="PKT_INFRA-LINK-3-UPDOWN ", SplitN(tag,"-",3)=["PKT_INFRA","LINK","3-UPDOWN "] so len(parts)==3 passes, then `atoiOK(parts[1])` on "LINK" fails and the line is dropped at logs.go:49-52. Every 4-part XR message dies there; the mnemonic would also be wrong if it did not. NOT rc1-blocking, and I did NOT raise the severity, because the drop is loud, not silent: Library.Parse (showparse.go:328-331) turns a zero-row Result into `Skipped=true` with reason "no line of the capture matched the authored format for this dialect — reporting inconclusive rather than guessing", and aiProjectDeviceState (ai_troubleshoot_deps.go:882-889) renders that as a StateGap carrying the redacted raw lines. So an XR log read degrades to a declared gap with raw output, never to a fabricated or silently-empty 'device has no logs'. No isolation, security, data-loss or RCA-fabrication surface.
evidence: logs.go:45-52 `parts := strings.SplitN(tag, "-", 3); if len(parts) != 3 { continue }; sev, sevOK := atoiOK(parts[1]); if !sevOK … { continue }`. No XR log fixture exists — showparse_test.go:947 only exercises DialectCiscoIOSXE with the 3-part `%OSPF-5-ADJCHG:` fixture (fixtures_test.go:455), so the suite cannot see this. Mitigation quoted at showparse.go:328-331.
suggested_fix: Split the tag on the LAST two hyphens instead of the first two: find the rightmost '-' (mnemonic), then the one before it (severity), and treat everything left of that as the facility. That parses 3-part IOS/NX-OS/EOS and 4-part XR with one rule. Add an XR fixture (`%PKT_INFRA-LINK-3-UPDOWN`, `%ROUTING-BGP-5-ADJCHANGE`) to fixtures_test.go and a DialectCiscoIOSXR case to TestParse_Logs.

rationale: Reproduces; http.go is untouched in d796bf7d..9d981e5e. The catch-all arm assumes 'every remaining refusal is a GUARDRAIL breach', but Manager.Start reaches it with two non-guardrail errors: `mintID()` (crypto/rand failure, manager.go:287-290) and, more importantly, `m.deps.Store.Put(...)` (manager.go:307-311), which on the Postgres store is a driver error. writeError (main.go:4549-4551) emits `err.Error()` verbatim into the JSON body with no Scrub, so a pgx SQLSTATE/constraint/table name reaches the caller, as a 400 that blames the operator for a server-side fault. Severity stays low because reaching it needs an authenticated infrastructure:write principal who can already see the device, and PG is only default for fresh installs.
evidence: http.go:174-178 `case err != nil: // Every remaining refusal is a GUARDRAIL breach … a.m.deps.WriteError(w, http.StatusBadRequest, err)`. Contrast handleList in the same file, http.go:207-211: `a.m.deps.LogError("packet capture list failed", …"error": a.m.deps.Scrub(err.Error())}); a.m.deps.WriteError(w, http.StatusInternalServerError, errors.New("packet captures are unavailable"))`. main.go:4549 `func writeError(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, err error) { writeJSON(w, status, map[string]string{"error": err.Error()}) }`. manager.go:307-311 returns the store error unwrapped and unlogged.
suggested_fix: Give Store.Put/mintID their own arm before the catch-all (a sentinel or an errors.As on the store error), matching handleList: LogError with Scrub, and answer 500 with a fixed 'the capture could not be started' string. Keep the 400+verbatim arm only for CheckBounds/ValidateFilter/ValidateInterface errors, which are the ones written to be shown.

where: src/backend/internal/pcap/bpf.go:68 vs commands.go:281 (prepareRequest re-validating the canonical filter)
rationale: Reproduces by construction; bpf.go and commands.go are untouched in the window. ValidateFilter bounds the RAW text (`if len(raw) > MaxFilterLen`, MaxFilterLen=256, doc.go:78) and then returns the canonical rendering `strings.Join(toks, " ")` (bpf.go:96), which makes every parenthesis its own space-separated token. prepareRequest (commands.go:281-285) re-runs ValidateFilter on that canonical string, so a filter that grew past 256 fails there. Worked example, entirely inside the grammar (parseFilter accepts it, depth 1, 64 tokens which is <= the `len(toks) > 64` cap at bpf.go:90): 13 groups of `(host 1.1.1.1)` joined by bare `and` -> raw = 13*14 + 12*3 = 218 chars, accepted; canonical = sum(token lengths)=205 plus 63 separators = 268 chars, refused. Manager.Start returns 202 Accepted with the row stored, and the async run() body then fails the capture via m.fail with 'capture filter is longer than 256 characters' — a length the operator never wrote. NOT rc1-blocking: the guardrail is fail-closed (nothing unvalidated reaches a device, the injection boundary is intact), no data is lost or corrupted, and the failure is recorded on the row and surfaced. It is an accept-then-fail UX/consistency defect in a narrow corner.
evidence: bpf.go:68-70 `if len(raw) > MaxFilterLen { return "", fmt.Errorf("capture filter is longer than %d characters", MaxFilterLen) }` — checked before tokenizing; bpf.go:96 `return strings.Join(toks, " "), nil`; bpf.go:102-123 tokenizeFilter emits '(' and ')' as standalone tokens; commands.go:280-286 `canon, err := ValidateFilter(req.Filter)` on the already-canonical string; manager.go:353-361 `set, err := m.deps.Commands.For(...); if err != nil { m.fail(ctx, scope, rec, err); return }`.
suggested_fix: Bound the canonical rendering, not just the raw text: in ValidateFilter check `len(canon) > MaxFilterLen` after the Join and refuse there (synchronously, at the 400), so raw and canonical can never disagree. Add a bpf_test case with the 13-group parenthesised filter asserting that ValidateFilter(ValidateFilter(x)) is idempotent.

rationale: Reproduces at HEAD — the line is present verbatim after cb406a95/39d6246f. `aerr` is tested only as `aerr == nil && found`, so a store read failure makes the branch fall through with no log, no metric and no note: the durable half of the gate is disabled and the code proceeds to mint an id and start a capture. The comment two lines above calls this the 'Durable half of the one-at-a-time gate', so the degradation contradicts the stated design. rc1_blocking on the SILENT FAILURE clause (§10 'no silent failures allowed' / §5 'no ignored errors') — the error is consumed and discarded with nothing observable. Severity stays LOW rather than higher because the exposure is genuinely narrow: the in-process claim at manager.go:293 still refuses a duplicate inside a live api process, and a store whose ActiveFor read failed will usually fail the Store.Put at manager.go:307 a few lines later, which does return an error. The gate is only really lost on a partial store failure (read path down, write path up) or across an api restart.
evidence: manager.go:280-286 `// Durable half of the one-at-a-time gate.` / `if running, found, aerr := m.deps.Store.ActiveFor(ctx, p.Tenant, p.Cross, dev.ID); aerr == nil && found {`. No LogWarn/LogError anywhere between manager.go:279 and 296; contrast the same file's own convention at manager.go:385-387 and 419-425 where every non-fatal failure is logged with Scrub.
suggested_fix: Handle aerr explicitly: LogWarn (or LogError) with `m.deps.Scrub(aerr.Error())` naming the device, and decide the posture deliberately — the safe reading of 'a privileged action on a production device' is to refuse the start (503/ErrInFlight-style) when the durable gate cannot be consulted, rather than proceed on the in-process claim alone. At minimum it must not be silent.

rationale: Reproduces at HEAD; the line moved (302 -> 401) when 9b7d12ca added collectOneGuarded, but the bug is untouched — `git diff d796bf7d..9d981e5e -- fanout.go | grep FinishedAt` shows exactly one added line, the panic path's `StartedAt: started, FinishedAt: c.now().UTC()`. collectOne's return is UNNAMED (`func (c *BatteryCollector) collectOne(...) DeviceState`), so `return st` copies the value into the return slot and the deferred closure then mutates a local nobody reads. Every DeviceState from the normal path therefore carries the zero time.Time in FinishedAt; only notRun (fanout.go:328) and the panic recovery (fanout.go:373) — both of which assign the field at construction — are right. The single production caller is aiProjectDeviceState (ai_troubleshoot_deps.go:847+), which reads Status, Note, Commands and Parsed and never touches StartedAt/FinishedAt; DeviceState carries no json tags and is not serialised anywhere. So nothing customer-visible is wrong today — but it is dead code that will silently hand '0001-01-01T00:00:00Z' to the first consumer (a per-device duration in the TAC bundle is the obvious next one), which is why it should be fixed rather than deferred.
evidence: fanout.go:395 `func (c *BatteryCollector) collectOne(ctx context.Context, dev Device, area Area, tgt Target) DeviceState {` (unnamed result) and fanout.go:401 `defer func() { st.FinishedAt = c.now().UTC() }()`, with plain `return st` at :406, :412, :467 and the switch tail.
